' DEATH OF liOTHSCIIILD. ( London Standard, Aug. 4.) Wc learn by an arrival that Nathan Mayeii Rothschild, the celebrated London Banker, died on Thursday, July 28. at Frankfort-on-the Maine, at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. He was only 50 years of age. His visit to Frankfort was to be present at the marriage of his son. His illness continued for several weeks, before it terminated in death. He was sensible to the last. It is said that he had a strong presentiment that he should not return to England þÿ but an impression prevails, that his life might have been saved, il better professional advice could have been procured than that found on the spot. Mr. Kothschild was emphatically speaking, a sell made man þÿ the rise of Ins fortune w as all within the present century. He came to England in 1800, w here he acted as agent for his father in the purchase of goods for the continent. Shortly afterwards, through the agency of his father, and the Prince of Hesse Cassel, he had large sums of money placed at his disposal, which he employed w ith extraordinary judgment, and his means went on at a rapid rale of accumulation. It was not till the breaking out of the war with Spain in 1808, that his extraordinary means, which were displayed in making remittances for the English army in that country, were developed to any extent, so as to be known to the mercantile world generally. He was one of ten children, eight of whom survive him four þÿ brothers, two younger and two older than himself, and four sisters. He married the

daughter of Mr. Cohen, a merchant in London, who is said so little to have anticipated the success in life of his future son-in-law, that ho entertained some doubts about the prudence ot the match þÿ and Mr. Rothschild was accordingly desired to produce testimonials as to his worldly means. The whimsical answer w as, that wha'ever number of daughters Mr Cohen possessed, he could not do better, so fur as money and good character went, than to give them all to Nathan Mayer llothschild. The death ot this eminent Banker is one of the most important events fur London and perhaps for Europe, which has occurred for some time his financial transactions have þÿ pervaded the whole continent þÿ and may he said to have exercised more or less intluence on money business of every description. No operations on an equally large scaie have existed in Europe previous to his þÿtime for thev were not confined to his own capiial and resources, which were immense, but were carried on in conjunction with his brothers in Paris, in Vienna, in Frankfort, and in Naples þÿ ail of whom possess colossal fortunes of their own. Besides which, lie hud agencies established in almost cverv large city in the old or the new world, all of which, undei his directions, conducted extensive business of various kinds, Notniug therefore was too great extended, provided the project was a or reasonable one, for him to undertake. All the brothers of Mr. Rothschild are men of great capacity and knowledge of business þÿ but it is

generally admitted that they deferred to lus judgment in all their undertakings, and thai lie was the moving principle of the great mass of capital they represented. M Rothschild like the rest of his brothers held a patent of nobility with the title of Baron, but he never assumed if, anil was more justly proud of that name under which lie had acquired a distinction which n; title could convey.

The choice of electors of President of the United Slates was over, and it is ascertained that Mr. Van Buren will receive a majority of the votes. The election has been however severely contested, General Harrison running bis opponent very close. In Pensylvania, which polls nearly 200,000 voters, the Van Buren majority is scarcely 4,000. In V irginia as large a state, the Van Buren majority is not over 3,000, and in North Carolina not over 2,000. In New York Stale, which polls 3, ">0,000 voters, the Van Buren majority is about 25,000, this is his native state. Ohio, Kentucky, Tenessee, Maryland, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Georgia, Indiana, Vermont; Delaware, South Carolina, and Alabama, have all chosen electors opposed to Mr. V an Buren, had the state of Pensylvania, or Virginia voted against him he would have lost his election. The electors meet on the first Wednesday of December and give in their votes for President and Vice President, the whole number of electoral votes are 2!) I, the successful candidate must receive 146 votes to lie elected, it is supposed there will be no choice of Vice President by the electors, it will therefore devolve upon the Senate. The Mexican Minister and suite have left Washington, in displeasure. Congress meet on the first Monday of December. A great money pressure exists in the U. A Fever Cured. þÿ Having read in some old book of travels or voyages, that, a sailor had been cured of fever by having cold water thrown over him, I proposed a similar proceeding to my comrades, to which they assented. With some difficulty I succeeded in crawling to the door (for I was unwilling to let any one touch me, for fear of infection), and a bucket full of water was thrown over ine. From late American Papers. ENGLAND AND þÿAMERICA. A late London paper has the following article on the growing commercial intercourse between England and the United States, and on the rising greatness of the latter. THE UNITED þÿSTATES. All commercial men must be well aware of the increasing intercourse between this country and the United States of America, The first houses in London are identified in bills of exchange with the leading houses in the United States ; and this they would not be, were it not for the great confidence which is placed in the solidity of American houses. The fact is that the States are daily increasing in their commercial importance and arc extending their connection with all parts of the civilized world. Free from national debt, their institutions all based on the broadest foundations, with a great tract of country to spread over, and increased in population by parties repairing there from all parts, and carrying with them what they have learnt and acquired here, they have every means of increasing in mercantile importance, and wealth as its inseparable con comitant. What is it but the growing commercial importance ol the United States that has caused the late sensation and perplexity in our money market ? The men who a dozen years ago were consigned to obloquy by the opprobrious terms of þÿ Yankees are now lifting up their heads on high, and are stretching their arms abroad. I am Gentlemen, your obedient servant, «<3C->W>» - þÿ O. P. Q Madame Malibran de Beriot. Madame Malibran was born, vve are told, in the begming of the year 1809. Her youth was one of unceasing study and harsh constraint. Her

father, the once famous singer, Garcia, and the best singing-master in Europe, compelled her to conquer a voice by no means of the finest natural quality, and to acquire a thcoreti. cal as well as a practical knowledge of music with a violence to which it is painful to advert ; and the audiences who have smiled at and applauded the brilliant displays of vocal power in which she revelled with unexampled profusion, little guessed how dearly such an

union of skill and facility bad been acquired. A simular education would have stupified or destroyed one of a less buoyant spirit, but Maria Garcia was sustained through it by a temperament of singular energy and vivacity þÿ perhaps by the consciousness that she possessed those gifts yet more precious than her impressive and penetrating voice, or her striking Spanish features, which were one day to make her the wonder and delight of all Europe. We have heard that in her childhood, she showed no remarkable evidence of talent ; but the circumstances of her profiting by and surviving such severe discipline, was no insignificant earnest of future greatness. Mademoiselle Garcia made her first appearance on the stage as one of that unhappy troop þÿ the chorus of the Italian Opera in London. It was in the year 1825, and, therefore at the early age of sixteen, that she made her debut as prirna donna on the same boards, in 'll þÿBarbiere. þÿ Her extreme þÿyouth, says Lord Mount Edgecumbe, in bis pleasant Musical Reminiscences, þÿ her prettiness, her pleasing voice, and sprightly easy action, gained her general favor. This agreeable impression was confirmed by her performances in T1 þÿCrociato, which was brought out by Volluti, at the latter end of the same ;cason Subsequently she appeared, with an increased credit to herself, at the York Festival, þÿ one of the youngest singers who ever occupied so prominent a post on a similar occasion. But it was not till her return from America (whi-

ther she had accompanied her father as prirna donna of his Opera company,) that her extra, ordinary powers made themselves fully manifest. We have heard, indeed, that so cold was her performance of the character of Desdemona, when she first rehearsed the part at New York, that her father threatened to stab her in good earnest, unless she threw more energy into the character. The threat proved effectual ; for assuredly her fault in her repersonifications of þÿ the gentle Lady married to tho þÿMoor, was one of redundancy, and not of restraint. It was during this sojourn to America that the ill-starred marriage with M. Malibran was contracted. The history of lias connection and its equal, are too familiar with the public to require firing here dwelt upon. In the year 1828, Madame Malibran appeared at Paris, we believe, in the opera of þÿ Scmiranii- I þÿde. It would not be easy to describe the sensation thenceforth caused by her perfor mancea throughout Europe, or to enumerate, the tributes paid to her wherever she went þÿ from the first garlands wherewith she was crowned at Paris, to the royal honors with which she was only the other day received bv the guard in attendance at the theatre where she was performing. For the last eight years our journals have been filled wiih tales of her successes and triumphs þÿ in one year gained Milan, at where the plaudits were so reiterated and tumultuous as absolutely to endanger the stability of the far-famed La Scala ; þÿ in others, won under our own eyes,

upon the well-accustomed boards of Drury Lane, to which sire introduced a refinement of music cultivation, a passionate but appropriate energy of action liiffierto strangers to English opera. We are not about to offer any cold or detailed criticism upon the merits of Madame Malibran as a singer or an actress; but a hasty word or two may be permitted to us. Jn bpth characters she was distinguished above ail he' contemporaries by versatility of power anJ

liveliness of conception. She could play with music of every sty le, school and þÿcentury. We heard her, on the same evening, sing in five different languages, giving with equal truth and character the intense and passionate scena from þÿ l )cr þÿFreischutz, and those sprightly and charming Provencal airs, many of which wer" composed by herself. The extensive compass of her voice enabled her to command the whole range of songs which is usually divided between the contralto and soprano. She was, it is true, often hurried away by the tameless vivacity of her spirits into flights and cadences which were more eccentric than beautiful ; we have heard her, in the very wantonness of consummate power, rival the unvocal arpeggi of De Bcriot's violin, and execute the most sudden shakes and divisions upon those highest and deepest notes of the voice which less perfectly trained singers approach warily and with preparation. But those know little of the dignity Madame Malibran could assume, or of the unexaggerated expression which she could throw into music, even the plainest and least fantastic, who are not familiar with her Oratorio performances ; þÿ with the euruiest pathos of her set. "a þÿ Deli þÿparlate þÿ(Cimarossa noblest s song;) with the calm and holy sweetness of her Pastorale from the Messiah, þÿ He shall feed his þÿflock, þÿ or, in a strain loftier than these, with her delivery of that most magnificent of recitatives, þÿ Sing ye unto the þÿLord, from Israel inEgyyt.' In þÿ

this last she so completely identified herself with the spirit of the scene, that no painter of M iriam the þÿProphetess ever dreamed of face, form, or attitude more appropriate þÿ more instinct with sublime triumph than hers at that moment ! The acting of Madame Malibran was marked by the same characteristics as her singing þÿ it was always colored, at times, over-colored, by the spirit which sustained her for a while through a career of unexampled exertion and excitement. If in no entire performance she ever equalled the siby line grandeur of Pasta, or the intense pathos of Schroeder, she had her moments of inspiration when she electrified her listeners bv out-bursts so brilliantly passionate as to make all her compeers forgotten. Her performance of Norma has been described to us as beyond all praise ; her Fideho was the best character in which she appeared in England. The concentrated and piercing agony of her speaking voice in the grave scene of ihat delicious opera is at our heart as we write ; in the part of Fidelio, too, her action was not carried to that excess which, in other dramas, at times almost seemed to threaten life or reason. In the opera liujf'a, þÿ as Zcrlinn, Busina, Cencrentola, Fidalma, (which last, be it remembered, she performed lu London to the Carolina and Lisetta of the Sontags,) her vivacity bad no bounds ; tier iS moijie, too, had the charm and the fault of caprices struck out in the humor of the moment. In short, upon the stage, though she

was oltcn extravagant she was always riveting ; and few among her audiences could go home and sit in cool judgment upon one who, while she was before them, carried them, as she pleased, to the extremes of grave or gay. The woman was one with the musician and the actress. The personal fatigue through which Madame þÿMalibran s high spirit bore her was prodigious. She had been known to go through the wear and tear of a five hour's rehearsal þÿ with a song at some morning concert between its pauses þÿ and then again in the evening, half an hour after going through one Of her exhausting parts, to be fuuud as ener-

And this again she would leave for some private party, where after singing with a freshness surprisingly little impaired, she would wind up her day's exertions, perhaps by dancing the Terantella# She was the delight of all her intimate friends, for the many gifts she possessed, besides those which made her so professedly eminent. Her observation was keen, her humour quaint and inexhaustible, and Her fund of anecdote various and always at command. She was skilful with the pencil þÿ some of her sketches are full of genius and character Her love of her art was intense and consuming ; and the circumstance should never be forgotten, (either as honorable to her memory, or as a warning to too exacting audiences,) that her illrie-s was exaggerated by her dragging herself into the Manchester orchestra to fulfil her engagements, rather than subject herself to the imputation of feigned indisposition ; and tiiat she exerted herself to comply with the fatal demands of a delighted audience, w hen the hand of death was upon her ! It is difficult to write calmly on these things þÿ and the thousand recollections that crowd upon us, warn us to stop lest we pass our wonted boundaries. It is enough to say, that, in the lyric drama of Europe, she who has died has left no peer behind her.

Death of Malibran. þÿ An unfortunate fatality seems to have attended þÿMalihran last s days. She hurried from Paris to London, and from London to Manchester, to fulfil her engagement at the festival. She went first to the Boyal Hotel ; hut upon learning that Lablache, lvanolf. Assandri ; and Caradori Allan were at the Moseley Arms, she removed to the latter Hotel. Her excitement began here, for she was not at all satisfied with pieces selected for her at the various performances. She essayed to change the programmes, but without success, for the Manchester Committee were not so plian.t as the concert and theatrical managers. Malibran was much vexed. In the evening prior to the first þÿday s performance at the collegiate church, she sang no less than 14 pieces in her room at the hotel among Italian friends. De Bcriot cautioned her against exerting herself, but Malibran was not to be easily checked in her career. þÿ The fatigue must have added to her already excitable nature. She was ill on Tuesday, but she insisted oil singing both morning and evening. On Wednesday her indisposition became still more evident, hut she gave the last sacred composition she ever sung, Sing þÿ ye to the þÿLord, with electrical effect ; and on that evening, '.he 14th of September, her last notes in public were heard. Her exertions in encore of this duct were tremendous, and the fearful shake at the top of the voice will never be forgotten by those who heard it. It was a desperate struggle against sinking nature it was the last vivid glare of the expiring lamp ; she never sang afterwards. New-Orleans, Nov. 11. The Money Market to day (11 o'clock) is a little easier, and business very brisk. The accounts on the Sugar crop are very

tions during the present month, from 90 to 100,000 hogsheads of Sugar may be expected in this market, besides the Molasses. Cotton continues to pour in in great quantities The remittances of specie from Mexico are trifling to what our merchants are expecting. The Mexican trade owes, at this moment, New-Orleans two million of dollars for merchandise ; hence the fears of an interruption ot trade with that republic, which I do not in the least apprehend, but the fact is, that the papers here are not well acquainted with the real state of affairs in Mexico. Yesterday they spoke of the rapid march of two divisions of Mexican troops to Metamoras, and to day they say (the Com. Bulletin and the Louisiana Adv.) with reference to Capt. Williams, that a division of 2000 Texians are in full march for Matamoras. This is all nonsense, the Texans were very quiet in their positions at Lahaea river, at the latter end of Oct. waiting for provisions, of which they were in great need. Five or six schooners have sailed from New-Orleans for Texas within the last fortnight with valuable cargoes, and a great number of passengers. As yet goods pay no duty whatever in that republic. These considerable exports are the result of the contemplated and necessary establishment of a tariff and custom houses in the ports of Texas by which means the Texan government will collect a sufficient revenue to meet their engagements The importation duties ore to be very trifling, from 5 to 6 per cent ad valorem, while in Mexico they arc from 50 to

The following is an extract of a letter from Lemberg, dated the 15th June: þÿ " The recruitment in Russian, Poland produces but few men in proportion to the violent manner in which it is carried on. The officers apply, without exception or any consideration whatever, the principles of responsibility and forced pledges which the General has established : and the inhabitants, collectively and individually, are subject to the greatest annoyances, without their producing a single additional recruit. M. de Novosilzcw adheres to his plan of exterminating the Polish language, and he is too well seconded by the Emperor for its not being carried into execution. Jn order to effect the dispersion, or rather the extinction, of the good Polish families, he has ordained acts that will scarcely be believin Europe. Numbers of Polish young maidens and widows are forced to marry Russians, and are carried into the centre and some even to the north. Young men, some under 16 years of age, are forced into the Russian service, and are not allowed, as formerly, to choose the branch they prefer. þÿ At Cracow, the magistracy has issued two fresh ordinances against foreigners, or rather against certain families which had obiained particular protection and permission to reside there from Austria. All this, however, is revoked, and Russia has evidently gained the ascendancy in that unfortunate city." A great Russian personage lias gone through Brussels on his way to London and Paris. It

is Count Nowosilzow, President of the Imperial Council, Grand Chancellor, <Sze. After the Emperor Nicholas he is the most eminent personage in Russia The history of unhappy Poland will record the share which M i\owosilzow took in the last events which have inflicted so deep a blow upon her nationality þÿ He resided at Warsaw, as Imperial Commissary to the Polish Government The motives which have determined the President of the Imperial Council to visit London and Paris must be important. Statesmen of that rank may, indeed, repair to rural residences or watering places for their health, but they d > r ot visit the great capitals ol Europe Without powerful reasons. þÿ La Paix.

The Congress of the United States have resolved, after long and stormy debates, to divide the surolus funds in the treasury ol the General Government among the several States> in the proportion which such State has contributed. The sum to be apportioned is thirty millions of dollars, about seven millions sterling. þÿ Is not this the first instance in the history of nations of taxes being returned to those who paid them ? The financial prosperity which such a transaction indicates, is owing to a really representative government, an industrious population, and an almost unlimited field of production. Let the people of England take advantage of their political knowledge, enormous capital, and extensive colonial possessions ; and the time may arrive, when, after an honest discharge of the National Debt, thev may divide the accumulation of surplus income among the several counties.

Washington. þÿ As the page of history opens to us the Father of our country, his character seems more and more beautiful, " shining brighter and brighter unto perfect day." Below we give one of his domestic letters directed to Lund Washington Mount Vernon, giving some matrimonial advice. Rocky Hill, 20th Sept. 1783. Dear Lund : Mrs. þÿ Custis has never suggested in any of her letters to Mrs. Washington, (unless ardent wishes for her return, that she might then disclose it to her, can be so construed) the most distant attachment to I). S. ; but if this should be the case, those who are at hand, and competent to give it, are at the same time the most proper to be consulted on so interesting an event. For my own part, I never did, nor do I believe I ever shall, give advice to a woman who is setting out on a matrimonial voyage, first, because I never could advise one to marry without her consent ; and secondly because 1 know it is to no purpose to advise her to refrain when she has obtained it, A woman very rarely asks an opinion requires advice, or on such occasions, till her resolution is formed; and then it is wish the hope and expectation of obtaining a sanction not that, she means to be governed by your disapprobation, that she applies. In a word, the plain English of the application may be summed up in these words : " 1 wish you to think as I do ; but if unhappily you do

I never expected you would spend the residue of your days in widowhood ; but in a matter so important, and so interesting to yourself, children and connexions, I wish you would make a prudent choice ; to which many considerations are necessary, such as the family and connexions of the man, his fortune, (which is not the most essential in my eye,) the line of conduct he has observed, and the disposition and frame of his mind. A Shf. Devil. þÿ A woman dressed in the garb of a midshipman lately applied to one of the Boston Livery Stables for a horse and chaise to go a few miles in the country. The woman in pantaloons was well dressed, presented her card with much sang front, patted the animals, looked at the curricles, talked big, and in short played the gentlemanly loafer to perfection. Of course the proprietor could not doubt the character of such a smart and genteel young man, and so without parley he ordered one of his best horses ana finest phaetons to be in readiness for his new customer. Off went the woman with a genteel crack of the whip promis.ng to return before night. Night came but no horse, no chaise and no driver. Another day passed and the midshipman was still absent. A third gone and day and night as before brought the same to pass, and the proprietor has now offered a reward not for midshipman, but for the recovery of his own property.

The fatal result of the system of immediate inhumation had nearly been realized in Brussels two or three days past. A Compliment for Bishops. þÿ As a Bishop was receiving from Louis XIII. the investure of the order of the Holy Ghost, and was saying, as is usual on that occasion, "Domini, non sum dignus " Lord I am unworthy of the honor " I know that well enough," replied the King : " but I could not resist the importunity of my cousin, Cardinal Richelieu, who begged me to give it you."

Suicide þÿ The frequency of suicides within a few months past, may not render it irrelevant to publish the following admirable order of Napoleon, w ritten while he was first consul, A. in which may bu pursued tbe solution ol his conduct after tbe battle of Waterloo : "Order of the Day, St. Cloud. 22 1 Floreal, ) 10th year of tiie Kepubiic, J " The Grenadier Groblin has committed suicide for a love affair. He was in other respects a good soldier. This is the second event of the kind which happened to the corps within a month. The first cousul publishes the following order . to the Guards. þÿ That a soldier ought to know how to conquer grid and melancholy þÿ that there is as much true courage in suffering with constancy the pains of the soul, as to stand unmoved under a buttery of artillery þÿ that to abandon one-sell to chagrin without resisting, or to kill one-seif to escape from it, is to abandon the field of battle before having conquered. Signed, Bonaparte and a Bessiures."

About the yeat 1758, there was a warm controversy in the third parish in Dedham, as to the location of a new burying ground- The matter was agitated at successive meetings ; tire opposition was violent, and the measure was finally carried by a small majority. Deacon Onion, notwithstanding his years and infirmities attended all the meetings, and was in favor of the project, and Capt. Baker was violent in the opposition. The Rev. Mr. Tyler, with his characteristic prudence, kept aloof from the quarrel. He conversed freely, however, with both parties, and endeavored to assuage their bitterness by his pleasantry and good humor. Soon after the final vote, he met Capt. Baker "Good niorninar, Capt. Baker. A fine day Captain. Well, they tell me they out voted you at last." " Yes, and much good may it do'em. This was too good a blunder for the parson to keep ; and so he steered straight to Deacoc Onion's to enjoy the joke with him. "Good morning Deacon Onion. A fine day, Deacon. Economy in Linen Washing. þÿ A correspondent of the Dundee paper writes as follows ; þÿ " After many experiments made by myself and others, I find that pipeclay, dissolved in the water employed in washing, gives the dirtiest linens the appearance of having been bleached, and cleans them thoroughly with half the labor, and fully a saving of one-fourth the soap. The method adopted was to dissolve a little of the pipe-clay among the warm water in a washing tub, or to rub a little of it together with the soap on the articles to be washed. The process was repeat" ed as often as required until the articles to be washed were made thoroughly clean. All who have made the experiment have agreed that the saving of soap and labor is great ; and that the clothes are improved in color equally as if they were bleached. The peculiar advantage of employing this article with the soap is, that it gives the hardest water almost the softness of rain water."

Iodine in Consumption. þÿ The external application of iodine to the chest is a mode of employing it, at an early stage of consumption, which I consider at once safe and efficacious. When an ointment prepared by mixing together two parts of hydriodate of potash, one part of iodine, and ten or twelve parts of ointment, is applied to the surface of the chest, especially over the part corresponding to that which is diseased of one or more lungs, in such quantities as to give rise to a considerable degree of cutaneous inflammation ; it will mostly be found to produce a great improvement in the state of the affected portion or portions of the lungs, provided its use be continued for a sufficient length of time. I have repeatedly found, after the continued application of Iodine ointment to the chest for some months, that the general local symptoms, & all the physical signs of the presence of tubercular formation of the lungs, were completely removed,, þÿ Dr. Little on Consumption.

The Queen of Spain. þÿ An evening paper states on the strength of a letter from Madrid, that Queen Christina has been for a long time married to her favorite Munoz, the ceremony having been performed by the Jesuits of La Granja. Three children are the fruit of the union, these are being brought up at Grenada, Bishop of that city superintending their education. Munoz is a man of simple habits, without ambition. He exercises, however, consideiable influence; the Council is often held at bis house, and his advice generally predominates. He is desirous that the Queen should withdraw from state aflairs, and go and enjoy the fortune which she has invested in the Bank of England þÿ five millions, and two millions more in M. Ardouin's hands, without reckoning the jewels, which Ferdi. nand left her, and which are estimated at several millions more. If matters become more complicated, she may be induced to adopt this step, but in retreating these reports we are far from guaranteeing their perfect authenticity. þÿ Courier Francais.

March of Machinery. þÿ According to the last number of the Mechanics' Magazine, a machine has been invented by one Mr. James Hunter, superintendent of the Leysmill Quarries, near Arbroath, which will entirely supersede the mason's hand-mallet and chisel, and leave all hand labor, in point of economy and despatch, at an immeasurable distance. Mr. Hunter calls this machine a power stone planeing machine ; and we are told that it is so ingeniously and judiciously contrived, that it will reduce and polish more blocks of rough stone in thirty minutes, at a cost of one shilling and seven pence, than a good mason could reduce and polish in five days and a half, at a cost of fifteen shillings and nine pence : and the machine, moreover, will do the work in a far more workmanlike manner than the man.

The dry docks of France, which but a few months ago, had ample employment in fitting out French vessels of war, destined, as was supposed, for hostile visists to our coasts, have been put to good use, of late, in repairing our own vessels. The papers brought by the Onatario states that the Constitution, the Ontario, and the John Adams were at Toulon, waiting to go into dock for repairs. þÿ N. O. Bee

Docs. þÿ Upwards of 3000 dogs fiavc had their day since the late Corporation ordinance came into operation. There is evidently a material thinning-ofl'among the species, though it is more apparent than real. Let the law once become inoperative, and our streets will swarm with them as before. A day or two since, we saw a man at the dog-bazaar in Wall street corner of William with a basket containing at least half a dozen pups, which he was desirous to sell' How he succeeded, we cannot say. At any rate, he was sure of 50 cents a piece, which by killing them lie could obtain from the City Treasury. The Exile from Siberia. þÿ An old sub-officer of the imperial guard of Napoleon, returned te Bouchain, in France, on tho 10th of May, from Siberia. He exchanges the residence oi 'I obolsk for that of the invalids which he is to enter on the first of J uly. This man, whose misfortunes recal those of the grand army, excites a lively interest ; he is 58 years of age but his sufferings had a greater share than age in wrinkling his brow ; his feet were frozen, and he moves with the aid of crutches. Being left for dead at the battle of Moskowa ; he was made a prisoner and carried off to Siberia, where he has remained 25 years, his misery as well as the difficulty of communication precluding the possibility of his writing to his friends. Having, however, procured with considerable labor a certain sum of money, he was enabled to quit the frightful sojourn which Russia had alotted to the prisoners of 1812. A few other French soldiers returned with him.

Beck, late of Island of St Thomas His Majesty's sloop Snake. It will be most gratifying to the friends of the lamented Officer to know that in a foreign land such distinguished honors were paid to his remains : þÿ « Extract of a Letter from a British Officer, dated St. Thomas 3d September, 1836. " Lieutenant G. P. Beck, R. N., late of His Majesty's Sloop Snake, who sailed as pas- a senger from Barbados in the Camden Packet on the 23d August last in a very delicate sate of health, died yesterday morning a little after the Camden left this harbour ; and the body was sent on shore in a boat they met a little way at sea. In announcing the death of this Officer in the Barbados papers, 1 would hope that an acknowledgement to the Danish authorities for the attention and honors paiu to his remains will not be omitted " The funeral took place this morning, and nothing was neglected that could in any way contribute to mark the respect of the Governor and the Garrison throughout the arrangements. The same honors were paid as to an Officer of the same rank in their own Service. The Governor and his Staff attended, and all the troops in full dress that could be spared from dutv. The whole was handsomely and decorously concluded. I should wish amazingly that this should get publicity, that the authorities here may see that their kindness has

not been unnoticed ; indeed, I am anxious that it should be done from being the only British Officer present, and 1 think it due from me on every account to publish an act of so much generous feeling towards the remains of a stranger to them and a countryman cf my own. þÿ Antigua Herald, October 8.

JDA5T3I& TSSTOTTMTJSL sma The Ourang Outang þÿ We translate from a late Paris Journal the lollowing notice of this animal. Many anecdotes are related of the sagacity and intelligence of the young Ourang Outang from Sumatra, which is now in the Muesuni of Natural History, lie not only possesses great docility, but he seems to understand many of the fei lings and actions of man ; he is sensible of reproof, and sheds tears and pouts when he is scolded. He imitates with great skill, what he sees done, and even invents appropriate means, well fitted to attain his end, when he meets with obstacles ; thus for example, when he was unable to catch a little dog, more nimble than himself, who had been given him as a companion, Jacco, (this is the name of the ourang outang) attached himself to the rope suspended in the middle of his room, and swinging, leaped in every direction till he caught the poor dog by his tail Another time he tried to open the door, like his master, with a key, having put the large end ol this into the lock, he soon understood his mistake, took it out, and put in the other end ; he loves children, carresses them, and takes them into his arms without doing them any harm. Ail this is the more singular, that this animal is, as is well known very young ; he is only tea months old and appears now near adult age, in the developement of his faculties. This indicates a short life and it has been thought limited to 29 or 25 years. We do not affirm this fact, since ail the zeal of naturalists has
been unable to clear away entirely the doubts which surround the history of this interesting species.

Russia trade. þÿ The trade of America with Russia especially in sugar, is much greater than would be generally supposed. The average quantity of Sugar imported into St. Petersburg, (chiefly in American vessels,) during the years 1832, '33, '31 and 35 was 25,000 tons per year, besides which considerable quantities of the same article were carried to other Russian ports, for instance Riga, Archangel, &c. In 1834 the importations amounted to 217,092,352 rubles, and the ex ports to 230,419,880 rubles. The exports therefore being considerably larger than the imports. Manufactures increase in Russia rapidly, and at no distant day that territory will be far less dependent on luxury and convenience than she now is. It may perhaps be worth mentioning, says the Boston Gazette, that more than one half of all the American vessels that trade to Russia
longing to any other port in the United States, engaged in that trace, belong to Salem. J

GEORGE ROBINS ANI) THE NAPOLEON RELICS. Mr. Robins has at length found a subject and a sale suited to his genius. He has had special retainer. The Napoleon treasures possessed by the late Mr. Barry O'Meara, and offered for sale at his residence in the Edgeware-road a few days since, were " items" such as do not fall under an auctioneer's hammer every day ; and Mr. R. instead cf wasting his sweetness on the desert furniture of Smiths and Joneses infinite, has been summoned to the forum to deliver an oration in honour of silver spoons, that might have inspired Cicero, and of silver forks, that might have tickled the soul of Demosthenes. The ear of imagination even now catches the sound of his hammer as the illustrious lots are one after another knocked down. A Turkish sabre with a real Damascus blade, worn by Napoleon in Egypt, was purchased at £15. 15s. An exquisitely finished portrait of Napoleon, by Abb' Lassaues, drawn early in life, seventeen guineas. A carved full-length ivory miniature of Napoleon sold at seven guineas. Of the plate used by Napoleon, a gravy spoon was purchased by Mr. Rotter, M P., for six guineas ; five forks were also obtained by Mr. Potter at £3. each ; six tea spoons brought one guinea and a halt each (the intrinsic value was about five shillings each.) A few lines of Napoleon's hand-wriing, a confidential communication from Napoleon to the Prince Eugene, was bought for eleven guineas. A small quantity Napo- of leou's hair, its colour light auburn, of a most silky texture, was sold for £2. 10s. The

magnificent gold coronation medal, representing Napoleon and Marie Louise before the altar on one side, and profiles on the other, for fifteen guineas, &c. But of far greater importance than all þÿ even than the Queen Anne's farthing, once the property of Lady Leigh's family, which sold for four guineas þÿ was the, it may indeed be called, the bone of contention þÿ the tooth of Napoleon ; It is thus referred to in the nairative of this memorable sale. " It was under a glass cover and seemed not to be much decayed. It was one of the three teeth extracted by Mr. O'Meara at St Helena ; one of which was sent to his mother, another to his brother, and the third was given to his friend." The learned Intrinsicator of Property dwelt much on the value of this relic. " It might be said, what use could be made of it; but he could tell the lad es that teeth in France were often made into rings, and he wanted to know what price could properly purchase a ring adorned by Napoleon's tooth." It was put up at a guinea, and knocked down to a Mr. Metcalf at seven guineas and a half. The instrument with which it was extracted was next put up, and purchased by the same gentleman at three guineas. On selling this instrument Mr 11. observed, his friend Cartwright was at present unapproachable as a dentist ; but he doubted if a man of great talent became possessed of this instrument, and took from Napoleon the famed tooth, what might be the result. Some of the commentators upon this event insinuate that the relics " fetched high

prices!" History were No, the prices may record otherwise. low, when contrasted with such high encomiums. It must have been worth- seven guineas and a half, not to posscssone of Napoleon's teeth, but only to see Mr. Robins display his, while expatiating noon Napoleon's þÿgreatness- decidedly " the

greatest man the world ever saw." " But," continued Mr. R., "now he is dead, and gone to a place where I sincerely hope he is happy ! We sincerely hope so too, though we are not made acquainted with the name of the place, and probably a good deal depends upon that. It is gratifying to see one great man thus stepping forth pay homage to to another. The Viscount de Chateaubriand, in his just published work, remarks upon this subject, observing how Shakspeare was appreciated by Milton, how Camoens was admired by asso, 'I and how Michael Angelo sympathised with Dante. Could he, by anticipation, have heard this eulogium, he would have crowned the catalogue with a note of exultation that Napoleon lias been appreciated by Robins And doubtless we shail live (if we are lucky) to see these names linked together, and to behold it recorded as the result of this sale, that Napoleon the Grand was emperor of France and Italy, and that Mr. Robins was the auctioneer who disposed of his gravy spoon to the highest bidder. It will be better perhaps that History should content herself with this simple declaration ; for it might sound inconsistent with the character of true devotion and reverence to the Emperor to say (what it must be owned is the actual truth), that Mr. Robins made Napoleon's hair go ofl rapidly, and afterwards knocked down one ol his teeth ! þÿ Court Journal.

A Word in þÿSeason. There ' is no evil habit, so utterly without excuse, as profane swearing. One would think that there is no temptation for an individual to transgress in this instance, not only the moral law, but also the rules of good breeding. Still it is strangely prevalent. We have met with an anecdote on this subject, which is worth þÿperusal. American Paper. A clergyman, walking upon a wharf where a fishing boat lay, while the master was uttering the most tremendous oaths, at length the clergyman turned to him and said ; þÿ Sir, 1 am acquainted wilh your business þÿ what kind of fishes are these I He replied þÿ They are codfish. Wilh what you bait these fish? With clams. Do you ever catch mackerel ? Yes And 1 suppose you bait them with clams too f Oh, no, they will not bite at clams. Then vou must hu\e uihciciit Kinds of bait for different sort ut lisli I Yes. Well, now, did you ever catch a fish without bait ? Yes, I was outlast year; undone day when 1 was fixing my line, my hook lell into the water, and the fool took hold ol it, and 1 drew him in. Now, sir, said the clergyman, I have often thought that Satan was very much like a fisherman. He always baits his hook with that kind of bait which different sort of sinners like best, but when he would catch a profane swearer, he does not take the trouble to put on any bait at all, for the fool will always bite at the bare hook. The man was silent. þÿ Anecdote or the Dure or Wellington.
I will give you a somewhat curious anecdote, on the truth of which you may þÿrely. Stimulated by curiosity, I rode up to a neigh I boring eminence, to observe the motions of

®3 ATE3 our own army, which had alieady commenced retiring, as well as those of the enemy, who, from the occasional pushing forward of their skirmishers, seemed intent on some further operations. On this height wore several officers, one of whom was seated, while his horse was held by an orderly dragoon, and the others standing around him I had approached within a few yards of them before I observed that the principal object in this group was Lord Wellington. In a moment my attention was arrested. He was at luncheon, and in the act of adding mustard to a slice of meat which had just been deposited upon his plate, when the following colloquy þÿ " place took The enemy are moving, my lord," said ; þÿ one of the staff officers to his commander, already busily engaged in the office of mastication. " Very well," replied his lordshipt " take the glass, Somerset, and tell me what they seem to be about," at the same time continuing his meal with every appearance of nonchalence. The officer did so for about a minute. " I think they are extending to the left, my lord." " Are they, indeed I" exclaimed Lord Wellington, springing on his feet ; " give me the glass quickly. He took it, and for a short space continued observing the motions of the enemy " Come I think this will do at last," he exclaimed. þÿ " Ride off instantly, and tell Clinton and Leith to return as quickly as possible to their former " ground In a moment all his staff were in motion. Lord Wellington mounted his horse and I

returned to my regiment, which, as our division was intended to form the rear of the retreat, had not yet begun to move Such was the promptitude and rapidity with which a decision affecting the fate of nations was formed by the master mind of our Great Commander. þÿ Blackwood's Magazine.

COO- New York papers of 22nd September pr. Bogota, announce the decease o! the celebrated Colonel Burr, at Staten Island in the 81st year ot his age. Colonel Burr was a distinguished officer of the War of the revolution, which terminated in the Independence of the United States; he was Vice President of the same during a part of the term of President Jefferson. In a duel with his great rival General Alexander Hamilton, in 1804, the latter was killed at the first shot, and his loss was universally lamented in the United States. Colonel Burr never recovered from the odium which the fatal result of this duel created against him. It maj' not be generally known that Alexander Hamilton was a native of the Island of St. Christophers ; when a boy of 12 or 14 years of age he emigrated to the Island of St. Cioix, and was taken as a clerk into the store of the late Nicolas Cruger Esqr. and shew so much ability and integrity that Mr. Cruger, whose concerns were very extensive, often went to America, leaving young Hamilton intrusted with the payment and receipts of very heavy Sums of money and the whole charge of his business ; which he conducted much to Mr. Cruger's satisfaction. Hamilton

wrote a poem on the great Hurricane of 1770 which attracted the notice of the Episcopal Clergyman of the Island at that time, who thought it a pity such superior talents should not be properly cultivated þÿ by his persuasion Hamilton then about 17 or 18 years of age was sent bv Mr. Cruger to King's Colledge in New York, where he studied about four years, and the Revolution then breaking out. Young Hamilton then full of Ardour for the cause of Liberty and independence, solicited and obtained a Commission in the army þÿ His fine talents soon attracted the attention of Washington, who made him one of his aids and took him, into his family þÿ at the surrender of Lord Cornwallis at York town, Hamilton distinguished himself by his courage and gallantry, and was promoted to the rank of Coloiiei þÿ on the termination of the war, Hamilton resumed his civil pursuits and embraced the study of the law. in which he soon rose to eminence, þÿ himself and Burr taking

on the adoption of the Federal Constitution in 1787 þÿ Hamilton bore a conspicuous part in the debates which led to it þÿ he was the first Secretary of the Treasury of the U. We regret to observe that the health of President Jackson, continued in a very precarious state ; þÿ h>s Physicians having interdicted conversation, fearing that a new attack of hcemorrage may be induced by it, and suffocation ensue. MESSAGE. Fellow Citizens of the Senate and House of Representatives, þÿ Addressing you to the last annual message 1 shall ever present to the Congress of the United States, it is a source of the most heartfelt satisfaction to be able to congratulate you on the high state of prosperity which our beloved country has attained; with no causes at home or abroad to lessen the confidence which we look to the future for continuing proofs of the capacity of our free institutions to produce all the fruits of good government, the general condition of our affairs may well excite our national pride.

I cannot avoid congratulating you and my country, particularly, on the success of the efforts made during my administration by the executive and legislature, in conformity with the sincere, constant and earnest desire of the people to maintain peace, and establish cordial relations with all foreign powers. Our gratitude is due to the Supreme Ruler of the Universe, and I invite you to unite with me in offering to Him fervent supplication, that his providential care may ever be extended to those who follow us enabling them to avoid the dangers and the horrors of war, consistently with a just and indispensable regard to the rights and honor of our country. Rut, although the present state of our foreign affaus, standing without important change, as they did when you separated in July last, is flattering in the extreme, regret I to say, that many questions of an interesting character at issue with other powers, arc yet unadjusted. þÿ Among the most prominent of these is that of our Northeastern Boundary. With an undiminished confidence in the sincere desire of his Britannic Majesty's government to adjust that question, I am not yet possession in of the precise grounds upon which it proposes a satisfactory adjustment. With France our diplomatic relations have been resumed, and under circumstances which attest the disposition of both governments to preserve a mutually beneficial intercourse, and foster those amicable feelings which are so strongly required by the true interests of

the two countries. With Russia, Austria, Prussia, Naples. .Sweden and Denmark, the best understanding exists, and our commercial intercourse gradually expanding itself with is them, b is encouraged in all these countries, except Naples, by their mutually advantageous and liberal treaty stipulations with us.

The claims of our citizens on Portugal are admitted to be just, but provision for the pay þÿ ment of them has been unfortunately delayed by frequent political changes in that kingdom. The blessing of peace have not been secured by Spain. Our connections with that country are on the best footing, with the exception of the burdens still imposed upon our commerce with her possessions out of Europe. The claims of American citizens for losses sustained at the bombardment of Antwerpt have been presented to the governments of Holland and Belgium, and will be pressed, in due season, to a settlement. With Brazil, and all our neighbors of this continent, we continue to maintain relations of amity and concord, extending our commerce with them as far as the resources of the people and the policy of their governments will permit. The just and long standing claims of our citizens upon some of them, are yet sources of dissatisfaction and complaint. No danger is apprehended, however, that they will not be peaceably, although tardily, acknowledged and paid by all unless the irritating effect of her struggle with Texas should un fortunately make our immediate neighbor, Mexico, an exception. It is already known to you, by the correspondence between the two governments, communicated at your last session, that our conduct in relation to that struggle is regulated by the same principle that governod us in the dispute between Spain and Mexico herself, and, 1 trust, that it will be found, on the most

severe scrutiny, that our acts have strictly corresponded with our professions. That the inhabitants of the United States should fed strong prepossessions for the one party is not surprising. But this circumstance should, of itself, teach us great caution, lest it lead us into the great error of suffering public policy to be regulated by partiality or prejudice; and there are considerations connected with the possible result of this contest between the two parties, of so much delicacy and importance to the United States, that our character requires that we should neither anticipate events nor attempt to control them. The known desire of the Texans to become a part of our system although its gratification depends upon the reconcilement of various and conflicting interests, necessarily a work of time, and uncertain in itself, is calculated to expose our conduct to misconstruction in the eyes of the world. There are already those who, indifferent to principle themselves, and prone to suspect the want of it in others, charge us with ambitious designs and insidious policy. You will perceive, by the accompanying documents, that the extraordinaay mission from Mexico has been terminated, on the sole grounds that the obligations of this government to itself and to Mexico, under treaty stipulations, have compelled me to trust a discretionary authority to a high officer of our army, to advance into a territory claimed as part of Texas, if necessary to protect our own or the neighbouring frontier from Indian de-

predation. In the opinion of the Mexican functionary who has just left us, the honor of his country will be wounded by American soldiers entering, with the most amicable avowed purposes, upon ground from which the followers of his government have been expelled, and over which there is at present no certainty of a serious effort on its part being made to re-establish its dominion. The departure of this minister was the more singular, as he was apprised that the sufficien-

ATC3 þÿ0 cy of the causes assigned for the advance of our troops by the commanding genera! had been seriously doubted by me ; and that there was every reason to suppose that the troops of the United States þÿ their commander having had time to ascertain the truth or falsehood of the information upon which they had been inarched to Nacogdoches þÿ would be either there in perfect accordance with the principles admitted to be just in his conference with the secretary of state, by the Mexican minister himself, or were already withdrawn in consequence of the impressive warnings their commanding officer had received from the Department of War. It is hoped and believed that his Government will take a more dispassionate and jnst view of this subject, and not be disposed to construe a measure of justifiable precaution, made necessary by its own inability, in execution of the stipulations of our treaty, to act upon the frontier, into an encroachment upon its rights, or a stain upon its honor In the mean time, the ancient complaints of injustice, made on behalf of our citizens, are disregarded, and new causes of dissatisfaction have ali en, some of them of a character requiring prompt remonstrance, and ample and immediate redress. I trust, however, by tempering firmness with courtesy, and acting with great forbearance upon every incident that has occurred, or that may happen, to do and obtain justice, and thus avoid the necessity of again bringing this subject to the view of congress

It is my duty to remind you that no provision has been made to execute our treaty with Mexico for tracing the boundary line between the two countries. Whatever may be the prospect of Mexico being soon able to execute the treaty on its part, it is proper that we should be, in anticipation, prepared at alt times to perform our obligations, without regard to the probable condition of those with whom we have contracted them The result ol the confidential inquiries made into the condition and prospects of the newly declared Texan government, will be communicated to you in the course of the þÿsession. þÿ You will perceive, from the report of the Secretary of the Treasury, that the financial means of the country continue to keep pace with its improvement in all other respects. þÿ The receipts into the Treasury during the present year, will amount to about $47,691,- 898 ; those from customs being estimated at $22,523,151 ; those from lands at about $24,- 000,000, and the residue from miscellaneous sources. The expenditure for all objects during the year, are estimated not to exceed $32,000,000, which will leave a balance in the Treasury lor public purposes on the first day of January next, ol about $41,723,959. This sum, with the exception of five millions, will be transferred to the several States, in accordance with the provisions of the act regulating the deposites of the public þÿmoney. þÿ The experience of other nations admonished us to hasten the extinguishment of the pub-

lic debt. But it will be in vain that we have congratulated each other upon the disappearance of this evil, if we do not guard against the equally great one of preventing the unnecessary accumulation of public revenue. No political maxim is better established than that which tells us that an improvident expenditure of money is the parent of profligacy, and that no people can hope to perpetuate their liberties who long acquiesce in a policy which taxes them for objects not necessary to the legitimate and real wants of their government-

Flattering as is the condition of our country at the present period, because of its unexampled advance in all the steps ot social anil political improvement, it cannot be disguised that there is a lurking danger already apparent in the neglect of this warning truth, and that the time has arrived when the representatives of the people should be employed in devising some more appropriate remedy than now exists, to avert þÿit. þÿ The safest and simplest mode of obviating all the difficulties which have been mentioned, is to collect only revenue enough to meet the wants of the government, and the people keep the balance of the property in their own hands, to be used for their own profit. Each state will then support its own government, and contribute its due share towards the support of the general government. There would be no surplus to cramp and lessen the resources of individual wealth and enterprise, and the banks would be left to their ordinary means. Whatever agitations and fluctuations might arise from our unfortuate paper system, they could never be attributed, justly or unjustly, to the action of the federal government. þÿ There would be some guaranty that the spirit of wild speculation, which seeks to convert the surplus revenue into banking capital, would be effectually cheeked, and that the scenes of demoralization; which are now so prevalent through the land, would þÿdisappear. to the demand ; and more than þÿ In reducing the revenue to the wants of the Government, your particular attention is

invited to those articles which constitute the necessaries of life. The duty on salt was laid as a war tax, and was no doubt continued to ges. assist in providing for the payment of the war debt. THE BRIDAL GIFT. A TALE. ( From the Plain Englishman ) There was merriment and rejoicing in the little village of Ifley, for one of its prettiest maidens was that day to be led to the altar by one of its honest youths. It was the season of temporary repose and of anxious hope between the hay and the corn harvest, which is perhaps one of the most interesting of the whole year Two or three clusters of villagers were to be seen in the church-yard, looking with happy haste for the arrival of the bride and bridegroom. Their smiling faces were in harmony with the universal brightness of the landscape which layaiound. The Thames, which is here but a little streamlet, was sparkling in t;ie beaming sunshine, or reflecting the few passing clouds of a summer morning; þÿ the cattle were grazing in the green fields, which were now free for their unconfined enjoyment ; the light breeze was passing over the ripening corn, swaying it with the most graceful and wave-like motion. The old Saxon church stood amidst the graves of twenty generations, a splendid monument of ancient piety. As the aged people sat in its spacious porch, they looked back to the lime when their hopes of happiness had been as ardent as those of the young pair, who were now approaching to begin the same course of domestic comfort, which they had sought in the morning of their lives ; and some sighed for disappointed expectations, and some wept for their departed companions. As the youthful lolks tripped over the green mounds whose lessons were at that moment forgotten,

they thought only of life as of one long summer day, and they looked at the happiness they were about to witness as something which might be privileged from the clouds and storms of maturer years. But the approach of the minister disturbed their reveries. Alice Holt and James Webb bad plighted their vows, and the bells of the old tower were pouring fourth that music which is always sweet, and the smiling gossips had strewed flowers in their wav, and the kind-hearted pastor had given them an affectionate greeting, when a reverend stranger stood in their homeward path and implored a blessing for them. þÿ The young people returned his salutation with natural politeness, and invited him to partake of their humble entertainment. þÿ There was something in the þÿstranger appear- s ance that on any ordinary occasion would have commanded respect. His dress was very plain but extremely neat ; þÿ his garb was of an antiquated fashion, but it seemed as if n > modern taste would accord witli the wearer. His long grey hair curled upon his unstooping shoulders; and his staff seemed ra. ther the companion of a vigorous man lhan the support of an infirm one. The stranger accepted the offer which was made him, and took his scat at the wedding festival without causing experiencing or embarrassment. Alter the cup had gone merrily round to those pledges of good-will which were much sineerer than the compliments of more splendid boards, the stranger rose to propose a sentiment. Adapting his language to the homely

garb in which the feelings of the other guests had been expressed, he exclaimed with much emphasis. May a good turn never bo for. gotten." The toast went round, but the stranger did not sit down. þÿ My þÿfriends, he continue d, þÿ 1 came here this day to pay a debt. Jt is of very long standing, but the obligation

©Airsx 'TastrtmaMtsx 3ias2ja-JJ2ir®3 A'tr.s. to discharge it is not the less absolute. There is a token by which that good old man in the chimney corner will remember me, hut that is for his own ear. I was in trade ; þÿ my means were small, þÿ and I was unfortunate. 1 sold all ; and I thank God I paid all that 1 was in debt. Without a shilling in the world, I de termined to go abroad. My resolution was acted upon ; and I communicated it to no one but the father of Alice Holt. On the morning of my departure he met me at the mill. He was the best friend I ever had He wept like a child at our separation, and þÿ excuse my own tears þÿ he thrust a purse into iny hands, which I believe contained the savings of his life. þÿ I long struggled against receiving the gift but be would hear of no excuse. My ; wants, said he, are few and are soon satisfied. A little more labour will make me once again as rich; but for you to be voyaging to a foreign laud, without a penny to buy you respect, I cannot bear it. Pay me if ever you should come home rich ; if you find me gone. I may leave a wife or a child that you may return it to." There was a deep silence in all the company ; and the bride was in tears. þÿ continued the stranger, do not think me an þÿ intruder upon your mirth if 1 thus cal! up the memory of the most kind hearted man I ever knew. Those are sweet tears which you shed, and you owe them to such a father. That happiness >s the most secure winch can afford to listen to the claims of truth and feeling. þÿ But to continue my story. Your father

left ten pounds my in hand, and 1 made a secret vow that no temptation of idleness or folly should prevent me putting his loan to good interest. 1 obtained a passage to one of our colonies. I engaged in a verv humble employinent ; but I gradually saved money. 1 rose in the confidence of my master, and my salary was increased. I at length obtained a small share in his business ; I exerted myself so much that after seme years 1 was admitted to half the profits. My partner died, and 1 stood in his place, opulent an British merchant. I at length came home witli more than 1 de serve. But my good fortune has been the work of þÿanother bounty s ; and I shall consi der myself a steward for my fellow creatures. Alice, there is the amount of your þÿfather loan, s þÿ it could not be returned at a better season. Young þÿman, continued he, addressing himself to the bridegroom, þÿ I have heard that you are honest, industrious, and pious. Your wife has her þÿfather features, s and, I trust, her faþÿther heart. s The debt I have paid will be a marriage-portion, not the less acceptable for being unexpected. It will stock a farm ; frugality and prudence will make it profitable to þÿyou. Alice and her husband rose to stammer out their thanks þÿ for the paper which the stranger presented to the bride was a note lor a thousand pounds. þÿ The wondering guests also rose with one accord þÿ but the stranger was gone. The bridal gift was not bestowed upon unworthy objects. James and Alice were not
intoxicated by their good fortune. They had abundance, and something for the necessitous.
SINGULAR INSTANCE OF SUDDEN DEATH. A drunken coal-heaver, near London, is related to have fallen from a waggon, and taken up and carried to St. Bartholomew's Hospital, He was stripped and the surgeon

examined him, but no injury could he discovered ; still he said he could not rise up in the bed. Mr. Abemethy was called in, but this celebrated surgeon could make nothing of the case, and directed that lie should be washed thoroughly clean, and a barber he procured to shave him. About an hour after, a message was brought that the man had, instantaneously, while undergoing the operation ol shaving, died. The barber said he appeared to be well and was talking to him one instant end the next was a dead man. þÿ I had hold of him.' said he. þÿ by the nose, end J did but turn his head very gentle to use the razor, when he without breathing or a sigh, went off þÿ Abernathy turned to the young students, and told them this was a cause for study, saying, There was a cause for the þÿman d s eath ; that the following morning he would open the body, and find out. At the same time he asked the students to think of the case, and tell him in the morning their opinions oi what might he the cause. One ol the students suggested that a vertebra! bone was fractured, and that as the barber turned his head to shave him, a splinter penetrated the spinal cord. AbcrneþÿAlice, thy innr, Jiately coincided in this opinion, and they then cut down the back, and discoveicd a small piece of fractured bone not bigger than half a pin, which had penetrated the spine : then taking the corpse by the nose, þÿ they observed as they turned it to the contrary, it entered the vital cord. The problem was now at once solved, and a striking illus-

tration furnished how little it takes to stop the great machine of life in man. An instance even more sigu'.ar occured in tiie case of a man who was found in a field quite dead, witii a hay- fork oi a prong by the side ox him ; iie was opened, but no probable cause of his sudden death could be discovered At length one of tiie surgeons sent for the fork in consequence of a witness saving that it was only a few minutes before his death tiiat he saw the deceased leaning on it, with '.he point upwards, as he was standing in the field. On the point of one prong of the fork was discovered something like a small speck, but no wound could be found upon the corpse. The surgeon now pushed back the corner of the eye next to the nose, and then declared that lie Had discovered the cause ol the man's death ; namely, that vvhi.e leaning on the fork be had slipped, and the point of it had entered the corner of the eye under the nose, and produced instant death. For,' added he, we all know' that in this manner we may be killed with a pin or needle, without having any external wound so as to indicate the cause. The surgeon then explained to the persons present, that this peculiarly vulnerable part could not be reached excepting only by th6 means described, that is putting the instrument used sideways into the corner of the eve, and then immediately direct it in a straight forward manner, so as to penetrate in a direction towards the brain, under the upward part of the nasi! bone. þÿ Such an þÿoperation, he said,
performed with the smallest needle, produces instantaneous þÿdeath.

Human Automata. þÿ The Russians when disciplined, become excellent soldiers. They are locomotive machines, which may be moved in any direction at the will of the officers þÿ The Russian soldier lias no opinion of his own þÿ his passive obedience and ability of suffering under protracted physical inconveniences, are almost unexampled. He conceives it to be his duty to obey his officers under any circumstances, regardless of peril, or even death. Many anecdotes might be related to illustrate the blind obedience of the Russian soldier. þÿ The following is from a work entitled Resources of Russia. þÿ Peter the Great at an interview with the kings of Denmark and Poland, hearing them boast of the superiority of their soldiers, instead of disputing the point with them, proposed an experiment, which was immediately assented to, and which was to order a grenadier to jump out a third floor window. The king of Denmark tried the experiment on one of his bravest and most loyal soldiers, who on his knees refused compliance. The king of Poland waved the trial altogether, conceiving it to be hopeless, when Peter ordered one of hi soldiers, the least promising that could be picked out, to descend the window. The soldier merely crossed himself, touched his hat according to form, boldly marched to the window and bad already one of his legs out, when the emperor stopped him, and told him he was satisfied. The kings were astonished, and each made the soldier a present of 100 ducats,

requesting Peter to promote him to the rank of officer. The Czar answered that he would do so to oblige them, but not to reward the soldier ; for all his soldiers would do as much, and by rewarding them in the same way lie would have no soldiers at þÿall. Sir Robert Wiison in his þÿ Campaigns in þÿPoland, relates that on one occasion a detachment being ordered by Prince Potemkin to take possession of a particular post, was met on the wav by another detachment in full retreat, and bringing the information that the post v/ as already pre-occupied by a numerous enemy ; and that to advance was a certain death; þÿ Prince Potemkin must look out for that,1 exclaimed the gallant band, and proceeded to destruction for not a single mau escaped.

©mts'z TE R R IB I ,E ACHIEVE M ENT. The Church of St Peter and St. Paul is remarkable for its spire, the loftiest of St. Petersburg. # # #

An anecdote connected with this church and not known, I believe, out of Russia, it is too remarkable to be omitted. The spire, which rises þÿ and lofty, light, and þÿsmall. and is probably represented in the engraving as fading away almost into a point in the sky, is, in reality, terminated by a globe of considerable dimensions, on which an angel stands, supporting a large cross. This angel, less respected by the weather than perhaps his h»ly character deserved, fell into disrepair; and some suspicions were entertained that he designed r visiting, uninvoked, the surface of the earth. The affair caused some uneasiness » and the government at length became seriously perplexed. To raise a scaffolding to such a height, would cost more money than all the angels of heaven were worth þÿ and in mediating fruitlessly upon these circumstunc.es, without being able to resolve how to act, a considerable time was suffered to elaj se. Among the crowd of gazers below who daily turned their eyes and their thoughts toward the angel, was a iVlijik called Telouckine. þÿ This man was a roofer of houses (a slater as lie would be called in countries where slates are used), and his speculations by degrees assumed a more practical character than the idle wonders and conjectures of the rest of the crow'd. The spire was entirely covered with sheets of gilded copper, and presented a surface to the eye as smooth as if it had been one mass of burnished gold. Hut 'iclouckine knew that the sheets ol copper were not even

uniformly closed upon each other; and, above ail, that there were large nails us.-d to fasten them, which projected from the side of the spire. Having meditated upon these circumstances, till iiis mind was made up, the Mijik went to tlie g ivernment, an I offered to repair the a. i gel, without scaffolding, and without assistance, on condition of being reasonably paid for the time expended in the labor. This off:r was accepted; loi it was made in Rus" sia, and by a Russian. On the day fixed for the adventure, Telouckino, provided with nothing more than a coil of ropes ascend u the spire in the interior, to the last window. Here he looked down at the concourse of people below, and up at the glittering þÿ needle," as it is called, tapering far above his head, but his heart did not fail him and stepping gravely out upon the window, lie set about iiis task. Ho cut a portion of the cord in the form of two large stirrups, with a loop at each end. þÿ suits The upper loops he fastened upon two of the projecting nails above his head, and placed Iiis foot in the others. Then digging the lingers on one hand into the insterstices of the sheets oi copper, he raised up one of Iiis stirrups with the other hand so as to make it catch a nail higher up. The same operation lie performed on behalf of the other leg, and soon alternately And thus he climbed, nail by nail, step by step, and stirrup by stirrup, till his starting post was uinlistinguishahlc from the golden surface, and the spire had dwindled, and dwin-
dled, and dwindled in his embrace, till lie could clasp it all around. »So iar, so well. Hut he now reached the ball þÿ a globe ol between nine and ten feet in aucuuilcicnce.

vastmraasst aatoiamastaa atis. The Angel, the object of his visit, was above this ball, and concealed from iiis view, by its smooth, round and glittering expanse. Only fancy the wretch at that moment, turning up his grave eyes, and graver beard, to an object that seemed to defy the daring ingenuity of man.
But Telouckine was not dismayed. He was prepared for the difficulty ; and the means by which he essayed to surmount it exhibited the same prodigious simplicity as tiie rest of the feat.

Suspending himself in his stirrups, he girded the needle with a cord, the ends of which he fastened, round his waist ; and, so supported, he leaned gradually hack, till the soles of his feet were planted against the spire. In this position he threw bv a strong effort a coil of rope over the hall ; and so cooly and accurately was the aim taken, that at the first trial, it full in the required direction, and he saw the end hung down on the opposite side. To draw himself up in Iiis original position to fasten the cord firmly around the globe, and witli the assistance of this auxiliary to climb to the summit, were now an easy part of his task ; and in a few moments more Telouckine stood by the side of the angel, and listened to the shout that burst like sudden thunder from the concourse below, yet came to iiis ear like a fain and hollow murmur.

The cord, which he had an opportunity of fastening properly, enabled him to descend with comparative facility ; anil the next day lie carried up with him a ladder of ropes, by which means he found it easy to make the necessary repairs.
LA MARRIAGE PAR LETTRE DE CHANG. In looking over some old papers, the following, apparently a translation from the French, was found.

A Merchant, originally of Paris, established in one of the French Islands of America, was willing to share with a person of merit, and not knowing who was to iiis mind, he bethought himself of writing to a correspondent of probity whom he hud at Paris. He knew but little of any other style than that which he hud made use of in his business, and treating an affair of love with the same manner as his other business, after having charged his friend with a certain number of commissions, reserving this for the last, here he set down: þÿ seeing that I have taken the resolution to be married, and that 1 cannot here find a match that me, you will not fail to send me also, by the lirst ship, a young lady of quality, and such as follows : Portion 1 ask not, but of an honest family, of twenty or twenty-five years of age, of a middle size and well proportioned, of agreeable looks, mild temper, manners without reproach, healthy and of a pretty strong constitution to resist a change of climate, that there may not be occasion to seek for a second it the first should happen to fail (which may we prevent as much as in us lies) considering the distance and the risk of passage. Arriving here in good condition, as above, and bringing back the present letter, endorsed on your part, or at least a copy of it, well and duly made authentic, so that there may neither be mistake nor supprisc, 1 shall oblige myself and engage to acquit myself ol the said hills, in

fifty days after sight to the icily that shall he charged with it. By virtue of winch i have signed this þÿpresent. The Parisian Correspondent read and read again this article, which classed, in some sort, the woman amongst the number of bales which he was to send, and after having admired the prudent exactness of the American, and the laconic style in the account of the qualities which he required, he thought to serve him according to his taste ; and. after many addresses, he thought be had found the affair of his friend in a young person of good family, without riches, of a mild temper, of a polished and cultivated understanding, well made and tolerably beautiful ; she was twenty-five years of age and seemed of good complexion He made the proposal with which he was charged, and the ladv, who only subsisted by the means of an old peevish aunt, and by whom she had suffered much, accepted of it. 1 hey were loading then at Rochelle, a ship for the Islands. The lady set out with tire goods, and embarked, being fitted out and furnished especially with a copy of the letter from the American, made authentic in due form, and endorsed by the hand of the correspondent. þÿ Without prejudice of the invoice of goods which he sent, the last article was in these terms; þÿ Also, a young lady of twenty-five years, of quality, figure and condition, specified in the bill received, as appears by these attestations and certificates, which she carries with her." With these writings, which were
