Ma. Riddle's Letter. Nicholas Biddle has addressed a second letter to John Q A ims, in which he treats fullv of the causes of the present pecuniary distress throughout the country. l ite following brief abstract ol ins remarks is from the Ad.ertiser : þÿ " A discussion of this subject, which at the present moment is of such paramount interest' by one whose full acquaintance with the subject in all its details, cannot be surpassed by that of any other individual, w ill be sure to invite attention. Mr. Biddle assigns as the main cause ol the einbarrasment, the mismanagement of the public revenue, in the mode of executing the destribution act, and the I reasurv order requiring specie payments for lands. He illustrates this position in a very clear and intelligible manner. He remarks that the amount to be distributed will be 36 to 40,009,000, m four quarterly payments through the year Ls37, oi which about 9,000,000 will be payable in January next. This sum lie says might have been dis tritiuted without and derangement ol tiade, and without the movement of a single dollar in specie, 'lo show that it might be done, he shows that a similar payment was thus made> on account ol the debt ol the Lnited Slates, in 1629, when the sum of $8,715,462, was paid by the Bank of the Uintcd Stan s, at a time of unusual pressure, >,,009,000 ol it to foreigners, leaving in the Bank, only $io4,265 belonging to the United States. 11c quotes the declaration of the Secretary of the Treasury
to prove that this was done w.thout causing ' any sensible addition lo the pressure, or even visible effect upon the operations ol the State Banks.'

Mr Biddle goes on to show that in the execution ol the deposite law, viz. the distribution ol die public lunds to sucli banks thai no one should hold in deposite an amount greater than three fourths of its capital, and the distribution to the several s ates, ought to have been performed. '1 lie true theory ol the case, he says was, to let the excesses of the revenue ill the several states bo transferred in the course of ti adc, to the great commercial points, and then to pay the stales by drafts on those points. I Ins he maintains would have been more advantageous to the stale, besides permitting the dci»osite banks to employ the money usefully to the time of payment; and in every stage ol Uio progress, business would

be assisted, commercial activity stimulated, and all parties be gainers. The Secretary oi the Treasury, instead of adopting this course, lias busied himself in distributing the money throughout the states, without reference to the business of the different sections of the Union, the season of the year, or the course of trade þÿ thus making the whole revenue of the country work against the whole industry of the country. This measure, sufficient of itself to disorganize the currency, was accompanied by another, which greatly increased the mischief, viz. the order prohibiting the receipt of any money at the land offices except specie. The operation of this order, which Mr Biddle regards as a most wanton abuse of power, if not of flagrant usurpation, is explained with admirable clearness. Its effect has been almost to suspend the commercial intercourse between the Atlantic states and the west» to pile up specie in the west where it cannot be used, while the Atlantic states are suffering for the want ol it. He exposes, in a strong point of view, the absurdity of the pretexts for this arbitrary measure. For a remedy for these evils Mr. Biddle recommends a removal ot the cause of them þÿ an immediate repeal of the Treasury order, requiring specie for lands, and the adoption of a proper system for the execution ot the distribution law. If the Treasury will not adopt these measures voluntarily, he would have Congress command them We shall publish the letter in our next paper.

George Washington and Aaron Bi rr. The following incident related in Davis's Life of Burr, shows the opinions which G» neral Washington entertained of the private character of Aaron Burr, and is a forcible illustration not onlv of the wonderful sagacity, but of the inflexible integrity of the Father of his country : þÿ " About this period the democratic party were highly incensed against t lie president lor continuing Gouverneur Morris as a minister to the French Republic. The Executive Provisory Council had requested Lis recall. He was considered a monarchist, and hostile to the revolution. Many of the opposition senators had spoken with great freedom ol the policy of General Washington in this particular. These remarks having been comnnuiicnti d to the president, lie expressed, informally, a willingness lo recall Mr. Mortis, and to nominate a member of the opposition, it they wouid designate a suitable person. In consequence of this suggestion, the democratic mrmbeis of the Senate, and some of the most distinguished members of the House, hail a conference, and resolved on recommending Colonel Burr. Mr. Madison, Mr. Monroe, and another member of Congress whose name is not recollected, were delegated to wait on the president and communicate the wishes ol the parly. General Washington paused for a few monicnls, and then remarked, that lie had made it a rule of life never to recommend or nominate any person for a high and responsible situation in whose integrity he had not confi-

dence ; that, wanting confidence in Colonel Burr, he could not nominate him ; hut that it would give him great pleasure to meet their wishes if they would designate an individual in whom he could conlidc. The committee returned and rcporteil the result ol their conference. The senators adhered unanimously to their first nomination, and the same dclc-

rjuj.r«j..'i -r7 gates waited upon the president and reiterated the adherence of their friends to Colonel Burr. Whereupon General Washington, with some warmth, remarked that his decision was irrevocable; hut immediately added, "I will nominate you, Air. Madison, or you, Mr. Monroe." The former replied that he had long since made up Ins mind never to leave his country, and respectfully declined the oiler. þÿ of man had for ages condemned their sex to They retired, and reported the result of their second interview. l'he democratic gentlemen were not less inflexible, and instructed their delegates to say to the president that they would make no other recommendation. On the third visit they were received by Air Randolph, secretary of stale, to whom they made the communication, but who considered it indecorous, knowing the president's feelings to repeat the message. This incident demonstrates, on the one hand, the strong and unchangeable prejudices o' General Washington against Colonel Burr; and on the other, the firm and unbounded confidence reposed in him by the democracy of those days. The anecdote is not related on the authority exclusively of Colonel Burr. It is confirmed by the written statement of a gen. man of high standing, to whom Mr. Monroe repeated all the details. ,\o other selection was made by the opposition senators ; but, on the 27th of May. 17!)4, James .Monroe was nominated as Minister Plenipotentiary to the French Republic.

Gov. Me' Duffle and Texas. Gov. iMc'Duffie reasons precisely as we should suppose any Southern man of intelligence would reason on the question of annexing Texas to this Union, and yet strange as it may seem, most of the Southern politicians come to the very opposite conclusion on this subject. We have never been able to perceive why the Southern Slates should be anxious to have Texas annexed to this country. It might indeed aflord them an opportunity to sell their slaves at advanced prices. But as an offset, to this, their own cotton lands would diminish in value by the vast field that would be opened in the sale of the Texan lands In short, Texas would coinc into immediate competition with the Southern States, in furnishing rice, cotton, and other Southern staples. On the other hand there appears many reasons why the annexation of Texas should benefit the Nortli rn Slates. We should open an immediate commerce with the Texans, and for their cotton should give them domestic manufactures in return. Thus would our ma nufacturmg establishments find an extensive market lor their fabrics, and our shipping merchants would derive the benefit ol the carrying trade In short it appears that if any benefit is to be derived from the annexation of Texas to this country, the advantages to the North will he greater than those to the South. Gov. Me'Duflie therefore takes the precise view of the subject, that we should suppose every Southern statesman would. þÿ Commercial Gazelle.

Constantinople, Sept. 7. þÿ The 4th Sept. will he chronicled in golden letters in the annals of the Seraglio, and, to all probability, its anniversary will be commemorated by the future generations of the Mussulman women as the uegira of their deliverance from the bondage under which the stupid cruelty

groan. In the earlier part of the day the Sultan sent for them to inform them that he had resolved on releasing them from the perpetual imprisonment within the precincts of his palace, to which they had hitherto considered themselves condemned for life, and on granting them the facility occasionally of seeking recreation out of doors. They might in future, whenever disposed to frequent any ot the public walks on the Bosphorus, freely acquaint him with their wish ; for he would feel it a pleasure to indulge their inclination, I' were more easy to imagine than to describe the pleasurable sensation which these words of the Sultan produced on his fair auditory. þÿ Their lord, it may fairly be presumed, at that moment appeared to their eyes as an angel sent from heaven to release them from their fetters They simultaneously thtcw them, selves at his feet, and bedewed them with heartfelt gratitude The ladies did not, it may readily be believed, employ much time before the toilette mirror. A few minutes after the reception of these glad tidings they were already embarked, proceeding with all the rapidity which the concentrated energy of 14 sinewy boatmen could impart to their light bark, towards llunkiar Skelisv. A strange coincidence must it, no doubt, have appeared to litem, that this ery sweet spot, where the Sultan but four years previous sacrificed his independence on the altar of Russian perfidy should become the theatre of the first ac t of their own emancipation The rapid move-

ment of the britsclikas and the loveliness of the valley they crossed, soon drove away apparently all gloomy recollections from their minds; for on their arrival at the delightful iviosque of Tokat they ail took an equally active part in the scene of merriment and frolics, which continued without intermission until the lengthening shades Iront the surrounding hills apprised them it was high time to return home. So enchanted were they with this day's pastime, that on their arrival at the palace they besought the Sultan to allow them to return to Tokat on the 6th , and did not desist from their applications until they had secured his consent.

AT!!3 Fair Play. þÿ A nobleman, living at a enstie in Italy, was about to celebrate a marriage feast. All the elements were propitious except the ocean, which had been so boisterous as to deny the necessary article of fish. On the very morning of the feast, however, a poor fisherman made his appearance with a turbot so large, that it seemed to have been created for the occasion Joy pervaded the castle and the fisherman was ushered into the saloon, where the nobleman, in the presence of his visitors, requested him to put the price he thought proper on the fish, and it should be instantly paid him. " One hundred lashes," said the fisherman, " on my bare back, is the price of my fish." The nobleman and his guests were astonished, hut the fisherman was resolute, and demanded that his request should be complied with. NEWSPAPER DEBTS. It is a fact, we believe, that Newspaper debts are held by a large majority of those who contract them, of inferior obligation to almost any other. It is not the less true, that upon every principle of business, and in the strictest sense, they are of as high obligation as debts of any description can be. A man pays cash for his daily food and clothing, and for all mechanic works. He pavs interest in advance upon his bank debtsj or his credit is dishonoured. So far from paying in advance, many of our friends think they act liberally if they pay for their newspapers at the end of the year ; and men, w ho plume themselves upon their punctuality and scrupulously honest dealing in other respects, will let their newspapers accounts run from one, two, three, or more years, if not called upon, until the amount of the account produces almost an inability to pay it, and not uufrequently a doubt of its accuracy. Now, why should a man pay his butcher or his baker, his tailor or his shoemaker, or his landlord, more willingly than he pays the publisher of a newspaper to which he is a subscriber? The butcher and the baker turn over their money perhaps fifty times in the year. The money received to day is laid out for cat. tie, or a fresh supply of flour, before the end of the week, which is sold out again the week following. A profit of ten per cent upon their sales may therefore be a profit of 500 per cent per annum upon their first outlay; a profit received day by day. How is it with the pub-

lisher ? He pays cash for the paper he prints ppon þÿ cash for wages þÿ for house rent, and all the contingencies of his business ; he lies out of his money, not for weeks or months, but for years, unless he presses for payment. At the low price to which competition has reduced newspapers, how is it possible for any one to conduct a business of this sort, without pay ments being made in advance, or at least with regularity, and at reasonable intervals? 7'here are those who suppose that newspapers yield a large profit ; we have even known some good people who suppose that the publishers of them can aflbrd to furnish them gratuitously, and therefore they never trouble their heads about paying for them. Some persons are even ofTended if an account is presented to them, as though it was intended to pick their pockets. þÿ St. Christopher Advertiser, December 27.

From the Barbadian, Aug. 20. Quarter past Three o'clock. þÿ We have only a moment or two þÿ our Paper being ready for the Press þÿ to express our sincere regret at the departure of our highly-esteemed Governor- General, Sir Lionel Smith. His Excellency arrived at Trafalgar-square at 3 o'clock, in a carriage, escorted by the troop of Life Guards, and accompanied by gentlemen of the Military and Colonial Staff, and bv public officers of the island. The Governor-General was received by the Royal Regiment of Foot Guards of Militia, drawn up in line on the East side of the Square, and two companies of the 86th and 70th Regiments, and saluted in the usual military style. His Excellency suffering severely from an attack of gout, was assisted by the attending officers into the boat of the Belvidera. Sir Lionel bid a cordial farewell to the gentlemen who were near him. On the barge putting off the wharf» the Colonial Artillery stationed on the Pierhead commenced firing a Royal Salute. We part with the Governor-General with sincere' regret, and wish him the enjoyment of every spiritual and temporal blessing.

It is a subject of painful interest to touch upon, but it is too true, that the town is getting extremely sickly. A fever, by which several persons, we understand, have been rapidly taken off, seems to be spreading about, and is increasing in violence. We have also heard of two fatal cases in a distant parish. We have been blessed by a merciful Providence with so many years of extraordinary healthiness, that we cannot be surprised, nor ought we to murmur, if the distressing period now approaches, when "the pestilence wafketh in darkness, and the sickness destroycth in the noon day."

it was most delightful to witness on Thursday the 11th instant þÿ the day set apart by authority for keeping in solemn remembrance the awful visitation of the 11th August, 1831 þÿ the uninterrupted stillness þÿ the sweet repose þÿ which pervaded even this densely-populated town. Except at the hours for going to, and returning from, our various places of worship (which were all numerously attended), there was scarcely a sound to be heard in our streets. There was, certainly, great external respect shewn to the day ; and we

cannot doubt, that all who remembered the heart-rending scenes of that dreadful morning, were internally affected with awful apprehensions of the Divine Majesty, then terrible in judgement, and with intense gratitude at the recollection of tender mercy in their wonderful preservation from a horrible death, or from grievous bodily injury. We trust none left our crowded Churches and Chapels, without the most serious and permanent impressions of duty. þÿ From the Barbadian Aug. 13.

TO BAG O. We have been favored with a perusal of a letter received from Mr James Ale1, Queen, dated oir Barbados, on board the Nightingale packet, 7th July, currt ; in which, after intimating his having had a dreary and protracted passage, lie states that he proceeds to Jamaica witii the charter of the Colonial Bank in his possession ; that after effecting its establishment there, he returns to Barbados for the same purpose, and thence visits the other Colonies where branch relations are to take place, so that he calculates he will arrive in Tobago on or about the 15th September, first. DEATH OF BAKKY O'MEARA, ESQ. ( From the Courier, June 13.) On Saturday last we announced the death r>f Barry Edward O'Meara, late surgeon to the Emperor Napoleon. The island of St. Helena has given to Mr. O'Meara a place in history, and when time shall have permitted all personal feelings to subside, history will do him justice. She will record him as a man of the most rigid integrity, capable of any sacrifice in the support of principle, and with a practical chivalry, defying power and welcoming privation, in the maintenance of bis proud Consistency. His was not the mere theory of patriotism: what he avowed he felt, and proved his sincerity by suffering in its defence. þÿ Power might have elevated, and wealth enriched him, could he have stooped to maintain a dishonourable silence where he thought the character of his country was involved. But he disdained the compromise, and the gloomy rock of Napoleon's imprisonment has borrowed one gleam from the virtue of its historian. To those who could not be misled by the partisanship of politics it may satisfactory be to hear that with his dying breath he authenticated the details communicated in his work, and has left in his will an inscription to that effect, to be recorded on his tomb. Thus, the " Voice from St. Helena" will be henceforward a voice speaking from the grave. A warmer hearted, or more sincere friend than O'Mcara, never Jived ; cheerful, hospitable, and uenevolent, charitable without ostentation, and at all times evincing a desire to

be useful to those he liked. He was a man of considerable literary attainments. He had contemplated a revisal of his "Voice from St. Helena." His fearless and generous attachment to Napoleon in exile, drew down upon him the hatred of the Tories, and it is not altogether creditable to the Whigs that he was not restored to his rank as Surgeon in the Navy. Lord Holland, as well as Sir James Mackintosh, were well acquainted with O'- Mcara, and with the facts. In private life xJ'.Vleara was deservedly esteemed by ail.

It was about seven o'clock of a hot evening when Van Pelt's exhausted horses toiled out from the pine forest, and stood, fetlock deep in sand, on the brow of the small hill overlooking the mushroom village of Saratoga. One or two straggling horsemen were returning late from their afternoon ride, and looked at us, as they passed on their fresher hacks, with the curiosity which attaches to new comers in a watering-place : here and there a genuine invalid who had come to the waters for life, not for pleasure, took advantage of the coolness of the hour, and crept down the foot-path to the spring ; and as Horace encouraged his flagging cattle into a trot, to bring up gallantly at the door of " Congress Hall," the great bell of that vast caravansary resounded through the dusty air ; and, by the shuffling of a thousand feet, audible as we approached, we knew (hat the lashionable world of Saratoga were rushing down en masse, "to tea." Having driven through a sand-cloud tor the preceding three hours, and þÿ to say nothing of myself. Van Pelt being a man who, in bis character as the most considerably beau of the University, calculated on his first impression, it was not ht advisable to encounter, unci' ansed, ti, if of fashion at that moment streaming through the hall. We drove round to the side door, and gained our pigeon-hole quarters under cover of the back staircase. The Bachelor's wing of Congress Hall is a long, unsightly wooden barrack divided into chambers, six feet by lour, and of an airiness

ol partition which enables the occupant to converse with his neighbor three rooms off, with the ease ol' clerks calling out entries to the ledger across the desks of a counting-house. Medical Anecdote. There is nothing which mankind are so anxious to preserve, of which they arc so negligent, as life. Cleora had heard of the fame of the late Dr. G y, the Scots Esculrpius, and posted to Edinburgh, to consult him about her health. þÿ As soon as she got there, she sent for the doctor, and talked of lassitude ; he told her it was owing to her journey. She said she had no appetite in the evening; the doctor ordered her to eat but little dinner. She complained that she was subject to watching ; he desired her to go late to bed. She asked why she became so heavy, and what remedy for such langor? The doctor replied, that she should rise more early,'1 and take exercise. She protested that wine hurt her ; he told her to drink water. " But my eyes fail me," said Cleora. "Make use of spectacles," replied the doctor. " My strength likewise (added she) begins to fail me ; and 1 am not so healthy as I have been.' " Because you grow in years," answered he. " weakness ?" " The shortest, madam, (returned the doctor) is to pay the debt of mortality, as so many beauties have done before you." " Learned physician ! said Cleora, (toss ing up her head) is this all the comfort you can give me ? Is it for these few simple maxims that you are so much renowned ? You have " told me nothing but what I knew already " Why did you not, then, make use of your knowledge? (replied the doctor) I pretend to no divination : If you want mysteriours remedies, you might have found them in London,

and have saved yourselves the trouble of so long a journey." His wife, after sitting for some time in the same room with him in annoying and gloomy silencc suddenly started up and taking a lighted candie, commenced a busy and seemingly anxious search after some missing object of deep and overpowering interest ; looked over the mantelpiece and removed all its ornaments, opened every drawer and closet in the room, searched under all the chairs, lifted up the rug, turned up the edge of the carpet, raked in the ashes' ransacked the tea-kettle, rummaged the cella. ret and repeatedly scrutinized the same places over and over again. At length, fidgetted beyond endurance, his nerves wound up to such a pitch of curiosity as to be on the point of cracking, his impatience absolutely boiled over ; and at last, after many severe struggles to maintain his dignified taciturnity, and positively unable to hold out any longer, he relieved himself by giving vent to the exclamation, My dear, what are you searching " after þÿ what have you lost?" þÿ My dear, I was seeking for your tongue, which has been missing this fortnight : and, if you had not found it for me now, I should have supposed it to be irretrievably mislaid. þÿ Anecdote oj the Family Circle.

THE LAND OF LIBERTY. BURNING A MAN ALIVE. The following account of the horrible scene at St. Louis, Missouri, in the United States, is communicated in a letter dated St. Louis, April 28, published in the (Boston) Loaning Gazette : þÿ þÿ 1 have just returned from witnessing the most horrid sight that ever fell to the lot ot man þÿ viz: the execution of þÿ Lynch Law1 upon a yellow fellow by the horrible means ot a slow tire. The cause of this unprecedented execution, I will now briefly relate. Deputy Sheriff Hammond, while endeavouring to ar- Test an offender, was, by the above mentioned yellow fellow, defeated in his intent. During the scuffle the prisoner escaped. Mr. Hammond than arrested the yellow fellow lor his interference, and took him before a J ustice of the Peace, by whom he was committed. þÿ While conducting him to gaol, accompanied by our constable, Mr. Mull, the prisoner drevv a knife and plunged it into the þÿconstable side. s Upon witnessing this, Hammond sprang at the prisoner, who now turned upon him and inflicted a terrible and mortal blow ; the point of the knife struck him on the chin, passed through his throat, completely severing the jugular vein ; he staggered a few paces and fell dead. The prisoner then lied to a yard or a passage way, but being brought to bay by his pursuers, and still retaining his knife, he swore he would kill the first man who attempted to arrest him. His pursuers, perceiving his threatening manner, backed out, with the exception of one, who seized a rail,

broke it over his head, which slightly stunned him, but soon recovering he resumed his menacing attitude, when a powerful and courageous man, but just arrived, seized upon a stone, and hurled it with herculean force, striking him upon the shoulder, and dislocating that limb. His arm dropped useless at his side, his knife fell from his grasp, and he was immediately arrested, bound, and carried to prison. þÿ Wc must now return to the dead and wounded. During the time occupied in the pursuit ot the prisoner, the news of the affray had spread over town, and the crowd around Mr. þÿHammond body s was joined by his son, an interesting lad 11 years age, of whose loud and heart-rending lamentations infuriated the already excited spectators. They swore that the murderer should not live another hour. This resolution onee formed they proceeded to the gaol where the prisoner was confined. Being too strong for the officers, who could not, under existing circumstances, make much resistance, after forcing three doors they readied the cell that contained the murderer, and led him forth amidst the shouts of the multitude. Some few endevourcd to quell the tumult, but to no purpose. þÿ

3&&RSR TBOTatSNMSR The friends of Mr. Hammond (and there were many, for he was universally beloved and respected), were determined on revenge a re- þÿ venge that may seem to you unwarrantable, but take the case home to yourself þÿ conceive your own brother in the situation of Mr. Hammond, and you will find some palliating considerations to abate the hoi rid character of this transaction. þÿ The mob conducted the murderer to a pasture at the back of the city, with the intention of hanging him up, but some among them cried out, 4 burn him þÿ! The horrible suggestion was immediately caught at. The moon had now risen bright and clear, the evening was calm and beautilul, too fair a night for the appalling spectacle that was about to be witnessed by at least 500 of our most respectable citizens. They chained the murderer to a tree, and the cry arose, þÿ let the fire be slow !' They piled shavings and rails round him until they reached the height of about two feet and a half, a match was applied to the shavings, and the murderer commenced singing a hymn, which he continued until the heat became intense, and then these few half smothered words escaped him, 4 God take my þÿlife. I had pressed forward, until i stood in front of the sufferer, I could not move þÿ it seemed as though some horrid fascination chained me to the spot, and I witnessed all his agony. þÿ Never matyr suffered more courageously. Not one single scream escaped him ; his chest heaved with the most intense agony, yet all he had said was, 4 God take my soul þÿ! God

take my life !' in accents so low that none except those immediately about him could catch the sound. He fiad been burning about 15 minutes, when some one said, 4 He fells no pain, he is too lar þÿgone. He immediately answered, 4 Y-e-s 1 d-o-f e-e 1 it þÿ! Never, never can 1 forget his looks, when with the utmost difficulty he uttered those few words. I he fire was so low that his legs and loot were burnt almost to a cinder belorc his other parts were to any degree affected, I he tree to which he was chained was in full blossom, and seemed to smile upon the horrid deed. The horror of that scene can never be effaced from my memory. Imagine a human being chained to a þÿtree a slow fire burning around þÿhim the boiling blood gushing in torrents from his þÿmouth his legs burnt to a þÿcrisp the life in me. yet his head moving from side to side, and occasionally a half uttered groan. But i will not, 1 cannot further enlarge upon a sight so horrible þÿ I feel a sickness at my heart, a dizziness in my head occasioned by witnessing that terrific sight; but 1 was rooted to the spot þÿ / could not withdraw my eye from the sight before þÿme.

The rule on which it is conducted is a very simple one, applicable to all classes. It is to allow no child the indulgence of an appetite or propensity, other than what is required by its intutive wants for its bodily support and health. Nothing is to be conceded by the whim or caprice of a parent to the imaginary wants of a child, for it must be constantly borne in mind, that every gratification of every scnce, whether of taste, sight, sound, or touch, i3 the beginning of a desire for its renewal ; and that every renewal gives the probability of the indulgence becoming a habit ; þÿ and that habit once formed, even in childhood will often remain during the whole ol alter life, acquiring strength every year until it jets all law both human and divine at defiance. Let parents, who allow their children to sip a little of this wine, or to just taste that cordial, or who yield to the cries of their little ones lor promiscuus food, or lor liberty to sit up a little latter or to torment a domestic animal, or to strike the nurse, or to raise the hand against mama, ponder well on the consequence. If they do not, often vain are the alter efforts of instructors ; vain the monitions from the pulpit. Their child is in danger of growing up a drunkard, or a glutten, a self-willed sensualist, or a passionate and revengeful ; prompt to take the life of a fellow being, and to sacrifice

his own ; and ail this because the fond parents were faithless in their trust. The states of Michigan is entitled to two members ol the House of Representatives, and the state of Arkansas one, who, together with two Senators Irom each state take their seats in the respective houses at the next session of Congress, making the number of Representatives 243, and that of the Senators 52. Both states wiij also, of course take part in the next Presidential election adding seven to the number of electors, and making the whole number 295. The number which must he given to a candidate to secure ins election by the electors will therefore be 148.

RUSSIA. ( From the Frankfort Journal of May 0.) The genius of the Russian people has up to the present time been either very lightly examined, or very badly understood. The Russian is a nation, or an assemblage of nations, as new and as bizarre as the concourse of nations which people the United States. Its primitive population is singularly homogeneous, and is of a common race, a common idiom, and a common faith. The Emperor, the head of the Church, and the chief of the race, is looked upon as the father ol all his subjects, whose devotion to him is unbounded. The world never before saw such a concentiation of power in the hands of one man. The Sclavonic tribes ar# simple and easy þÿ they wish for a master, and their submission is neither forced nor fictitious they love the yoke. Every age, by assuring the success of the undertakings of Russia' increases the devotedness of which we speak Let it not be said that the Russians are barbarians ; let not this multitude of men be branded as savages, whom civilization has as yet lelt unpolished and unprepared. Wonderful instruments in the hands of a conqueror : þÿ to govern them there is 110 need either of Police, or Deputies, or Peers, or Elections, or Ministerial intrigues. The whole machine is of the most extraordinary simplicity ; it works of itself ; and all the energy of this great kingdom is tree to be employed on the exterior þÿ the interior does not give it the smallest trouble. When the principal chiefs of the aristocratic opposition hav e

been once drawn into the higher grades of the army, Russia can march onward without ever looking behind. It is this that sets in motion the springs of her diplomacy þÿ a diplomacy so constant, so vigorous, and so enlightened : it is this that gives Iter talent to turn to her own advantage every event in foreign nations þÿ a talent which is worth more to her than conquest, and more efficacious than victorious armies. Having her desires always bent upon the accomplishment of one object, well acquainted with the East of which she holds the key, familiar also with the genius of the Turkish people, which we do not understand, and upon which nothing has enlightened us. Russia has made our diplomatists, and their profoundest combinations and master-strokes of design, the sport of her policy and the instruments ol her greatness. How was it possible for Russia to avoid mixing foreign policy in ? In remaining inclosed within her primitive boundaries, she would have been at the mercy of all Europe. Two straits, the Bosphorous and the Dardanelles, could give the law to her rivers, to her ports, and to her most important arsenals. These formed the double outlet for her wealth, and the double gates ol' her prison þÿ it was by these that she respired, by these that her commerce flourished, and by these alone that she could be extinguished. It is not necessary to be a profound diplomatist to understand these things þÿ it is sufficient to be a Russian. þÿ Vulnerable in these to points at a distance

from herself, it would seem that her vitality was outside, if we may so express it, of her territory. Thus it is that she springs to the succour of these dangerous points þÿ thus it is that, leav ing her interior civilization to take care of itself,, she remains ever on the watch. The first soldier of fortune who is sent as ambassador to Constantinople immediately comprehends her position. It is necessary

JBAR81E asWf»®SaU£ that Russia should be of weight in the balance of European power ; and she must not be niggardly of the gold which bribes and cor. rupts, but at the same time she will not spread abroad too many menaces or promises, or too much terror or gold. The first care of Russia has been to assure to herself the tree passage of these two straits, and she has then tried to weaken other Bowers, and to prevent a coalition against þÿherself a coalition which would ruin her. Her ulterior object is to become mistress at the same time oj the Bosphorus etnd the Dardanelles ; of the Dardanelles especially' which open out a whole world to her. It must be said circumstances are very favourable to her, and Russia is not ignorant of it. The model of an absolute power, she finds friends and allies in the most of the Powers of Europe, who see their authority endangered by popular þÿ usurpations, or, if you will, by the liberal ideas. Politically speaking, all these kingdoms find themselves engaged in an interior struggle, from the danger of which Russia has escaped. Morally, Russia offers to these kingdoms a model, an asylum, a hope, and a resource. Admire the language of Russia even towards England, her most redoubtable foe. The Gazette of Moscow, of the 27 th December, 1832, says : þÿ " The Russian nation is tilled with indignation at the secret part which England, or rather her perfidious Ministry, Itas taken in the troubles of Poland- But we will have our turn ; we will take off her mask, and will teach the world in what manner a

great people is rescued from slavery. You will soon see whether Ponsonby said rightly, in repeating to all that were w ailing to listen that Russia was nothing, and that her Asiatic Government should no longer be of any w eight in the destinies of Europe. How dares this indebted Albion to wake the Polar Bear (it is by this name that she designates us) this bear, which was well nigh devouring Napoleon with the first army w hich was fool hardy enough to set foot on her territory and which then proceeded to Pans to be revenged for this temerity ? No, the turn of England must soon come ; in a short time we must make no treaty with that people, except Calcutta. at þÿ Her false policy has played its last game ; and she may now go on and from an alliance with the negroes ol Africa, to whom she wishes to do so much good, and for whom Europe is her dupe. \Vc Russians, barbarians and slaves, as her journals call us, will one day give her a lesson In the mean time let them continue þÿ it is all we desire." We will not occupy ourselves further with the Asiatic possessions of Russia, but will content ourselves with the refutation of an error, shared by many politicians. The extent of territory no moie weakens the central authoþÿ rity than the augmentation of capital impoverishes its possessor. This is a practical question. We must know how to employ capital, and we must also know how to make the most of extent of territory at the same lime that we govern it. This immense domain of Russia, over which w ander so many name-

less tribes, is easier to govern than Modenn, a poor little principality about as large as one's band ! It is submitted to a surveillance socxact arid so rigid, that not a day passes that the authorities do not examine a space as long as the wall of China, to see whether sward bi urs the impress of the foot of a man. As regards European Russia, it is composed of immense plait s, which would ofler neither asylum nor resource to revolt, if the idea of it ever penetrated into a Russian brain. Place the point

ATJL3. of a compass on the city of Moscow, and form a circle, of which the diameter shall be one hundred and fifty German miles (fiOO English)» & within this vastsphere youvvillnot enclose its a single mountain or even a hill. The hollow of the valleys is the cradle of independence, and the summit of the mountains is the throne, ill en hide themselves in caverns and escape from their oppressors through the defiles of the mountains. Clanship and family spirit nourish pride and courage, but an agricultural population, spread over an immense plain surface, easily tails into servitude. It is more difficult to conquer a tribe of Bedouins than to keep under two millions and a half of Egyptians. And notwithstanding, when these last, incapable as they are of maintaining their independence, were led to war, they shook the Ottoman throne. The Bedouin remains a wanderer because he cherishes his independence. The plains of Russia, which feed the Russian troops, may be calculated at five hundred thousand square leagues, and the population daily augments more rapidily than in any other European States. During six months of the year the soil-refuses every species of vegetation. The Government lias only to give the order, and the storehouses full of corn wiil be emptied, the huts and the stable ravaged, and the peasant be left entirely without resources. Thus the peasant has not the thought of resisting any order. The being who, like the Emperor, possesses a power so complete, and we may almost say so supernatural, be-

comes, as it were, a god to his imagination. þÿ Ilis only religion is to obey. This universal sentiment speedily assumes a character of enthusiasm and fanaticism. In our days few Christians are to be found capable of undergoing martyrdom for their God, with the joy the Monjiek feels when condemned to undergo torture and death in obedience to the commands of the Emperor. If there are in Russia some few hard, intractable, and stubborn spirits who arc filled with European doctrines, they are immediately sent to join the army, where military discipline soon bends or breaks them. As regards the rest of the population, fatalists, w ithout embarassing themselves about fatalism resigned to all, careless of the future, without property, without liberty, and without hoprs, certain of obtaining either from charitv or from dispotism the necessary aliments of life, inditlcrcnt also as to the spot where thov may he allowed to subsist, they have no other w ill t ian that of the Autocrat þÿ no other joy than his good pleasure, and no other grandeur than in his conquests. This population, so useful and so þÿpliant this dough, so well kneaded (it we may be forgiven the expression) is composed thirty-flour millions of souls. In of other countries you find one or two elements of despotism, with a few feeble germs of liber ty ; but in Russia everything tends to ilie aggra ndisemt nt of this despotism, and to the furtherance of its þÿdesigns religion, manners, climate, oil, the past and the future.

- _ wTwr SMMM tmK XM3» mr '.Mi t ./mbr. amtsK Manner of Living at Ghent. þÿ Client is, I should suppose, one of the cheapest and most plentiful places to live in on the Continent of Europe. One fact is better than many assertions. I shall give the history ol a day in regard to the necessaries ol eating drinking, and accommodation lor the night: and 1 state the cost that rny readers may judge for themselves. In the morning from eight to ten, was breakfast. It consisted of cafe nu lait and bread and butter. The coffee was sent on the table in a large brass jug, one of those vessels to be seen in every old Flemish picture, and the boiled miile in an other of the same description. There might be about a gallon of the clarified fluid in the former, the other contained perhaps half that quantity. Three or four large cakes of a sweet brownish bread, each weighing about five or six pounds, were placed at irregular intervals down the long table, and about double the number of plates of exquisite Dutch butter intervened between them. The only rule observed at this meal was "cut and come a<ain." © It was the individual's own fault, bad he the appetite of a famished wolf, if ho did not satisfy it. The dinner, a much more imposingand important meal, succeeded at two o'clock. We sat down to table, a motley group, twenty-four in number, in a spacious and reaily handsome saloon. The dinner consisted of the following viands ; first, hot soup and bread, which was tolerable. The fault of these people is that they only half

make their soup, that they may eat the bouille as a separate dish consequently. Secondly, the bouille with a delicious smail greens, known, I believe, by the name of Brussels sprouts. The bouille was eatable, inasmuch as the quality of the meat which composed it was excellent. Thirdly, slices of cold corned beef, of an exquisite flavour, with apnragus and butter sauces. Forthlv, large halls of forced meat, made principally, 1 believe, of veal, with a sweet sauce the composition of which 1 know not ; excellent potatoes accompanied this course, which was altogether one that even an epicure might enjoy. Fifthly roast veal, fillet and loin, with a fresh supply of Brussels sprouts, asparagus, and potatoes, and a fresh sauce. Sixthly, game; this was i cally delicious. Seventhly, a largo tart and sweet cakes. Eiglitly, pears and þÿapples. Ninthly, bread and cheese. A pint of capital Feer was the allowance with this dinner. Wo dined off a very handsome service ol china ; had the luxury of silver forks and spoons ; and were well attended. The host headed the table, and helped every one abundantly þÿ Supper at eight o'clock closed the day It consisted of salad þÿ an excellent salad it was ; cold boiled beef sliced, with hot potatoes ; veal ragout, and beef cutlets, with excellent gravy sauce ; apples and pears ; bread, butter, and cheese. A pint of beer was the allowance at this ineal also. I never saw a greater abundance of eatables than was served up on these occasions; twice the quantity

consumed was removed from table at each meal ; yet all the guests were young men, and most of them pedestrian travellers, both ol' which circumstances tend very much to sharpen the appetite and strengthen the digestive powers. I had a small room about ten feet square, with a large folding window, and a very good bed to myself. It is true the chamber was not an elegant one, but it was perfectly comfortable. For all these I paid the sum of one franc and a half, somewhere about one shilling and two-pence three tarthings. 1

The relentless jackass still gave chase, calling to the fair fugitive with an occasional yec-liavv ! to halt ami surrender At length lie seized her by that prominent deformity which ladies call a bustle' tearing the ' skirts of her gown and udder garments away from her body. Matrimony by the Dozen. þÿ At the collogi. ate church of Manchester, on a late Sundav, seventy couple were united in matrimony and on the Monday following one hundred and fifty couples were tied together for better for worse. The following is the whole-sale mode in which the business is dispatched : The parties are arranged into couples of twelve; when the time arrives for slipping the ring on the fingers of the brides, the word of command is given, and the bridegrooms are seen busily feeling in their pockets fo, the symbol of endless affection; the women arc then requested to repeat the words of the minister, which they, "nothing loth," never fail to do; then the men are requested to follow the example, and their gallantry prompts them to immediate obedience. þÿ Glasgow llerald.

LOVE'S REPROACH ; a rustic flaint. tiy james kennedy, esq. Dear Tom, my brave, free-hearted lad, Where'er you go God bless you ! You'd better speak than wish you had, If love for me distress you. To me, they say, your thoughts incline, And possibly they may so ; Then once for all, to quiet mine, Tom, if you love me, say so.

On that sound heart, and manly frame Sits lightly sport or labor, Good hnmour'd, frank, and still the same, To parent, friend, or neighbor. Then why postpone, your love to own For me from day to day so, And let me whisper still alone, « Tom, if you love me, say so,"

How oft when I was siok, or sad With some remembered folly, The sight of you has made me glad. þÿ And then most melancholy ! « Ah ! why will thoughts of one so good , By you it should be understood Upon my spirits prey so ? þÿ " Tom. if you love me, say so."

Last Monday, at the cricket match, No rival stood before you ; In harvest time, for quick despatch The farmers all adore you ; And evermore your praise they sing, Though one thing you delay so, And I sleep lightly, murmuring " Tom, if you love me, say so."

Whate'er of yours you chance to seek, Almost before you breathe it, I bring with blushes on my cheek, And all my souls goes with it. Why thank me, then, with voice so low, And faltering turn away so? When next you come, before you go, Tom, if you love me, say so, When Jasper Wild beside the brook, Resentful round us lowered, I oft recall that lion-look That quelled the savage coward. Bold words and free you utter'd then, Would they could find their way so, When these moist eyes so plainly mean " Tom if you love me, say so " My friends, tis true, are well to do, ' And you are poor and friendless ; All no ! for they are rich in you, Their happiness is endless. You never let them shed a tear, Save that on you they weigh so ; There's one might bring you better cheer, " Tom, if you love me, say so."

My uncle's legacy is all For you Tom, when you choose it ; In better hands it cannot fall, Or better trained to use it. I'll wait for years ; but let me not Nor woo'd nor plighted stay so ; Since wealth and worth make even lot Tom, if you love me say so.

Natural Requisites for the Learned Professions þÿ " Na, I'm grieved io think about thae callants, o' ours," said the careful mother of three promising young men, to the sagacious father ; I'm grieved to think about " them, for 1 muckle doubt we'll never be able to inakeony thing wiselike o' them." " Never fash your thoom about the cellants, Janet," said the old man ; there's nae fear o' the caliants ; we's give them lair, and that'll set them on their feet. Nac doubt Charlie is a run de'il, and owre coorse and furysome a fallow to make a wright, or a weaver, or a tailor o' him ; but he'll do for a doctor þÿ for though he could na be trusted to work amang dear mahogany, nor to handle fykie warp and waft, nor to rin the shears through guid braid claith he'll do weel enough for physicking þÿ and the setting o' banes. As for Jock, there's nae denying that he's a loopy, sneck drawing, pawky scooncral, and no inclined to win his bread at honest calling þÿ but wi' a tift o' lair in his head, he'll make a capital lawyer, and answer weel for the dispensing ©justice. þÿ And though as ye ken, Tarn is but a fule, wi' as little sense or gumption as a sookin turkey and no fit to learn ony trade like a wisebody þÿ we'll put him through the college, tied lien he comes out he'll be qualified to get a kirk, and to be a teacher o' the people. þÿ Ayr Observer.

squaring the circle. A person in the neighbourhood of Bradford supposing he had found the exact quadrature ef the circle, solicited an examination of his method, by the scientific world. Finding anon that another was received with like courtesy, and then a thiid, he grew very angry : 1 thought," said he, I " " had found a friend's house, but I am fallen into an inn, to entertain all comers, rather than a lodging for some private and especial friends." On this storv, the admirable Hales thus expresses himself. Let it not offend any, that " I have made Christianity rather an inn, to receive all, than a private house, to receive some few ; for so both precept and example teach us to extend our good offices not to this or that man, but to mankind ; like the sun, which ariseth not on this or that nation, but on all the world. J ulian observes of the fig-tree, that above all tress, it is most capable of grafts and scions of other kinds, so far as that all variety will be brought to take nourishment from one stool. Beloved, a christian must be like unto Julian's fig-tree, so universally com passionate, that so all sorts of grafts, by a kind of Christian inoculation, may be brought to draw life and nourishment from his root" þÿ Hales.

The heart may be engaged in a little business, as much, if thou watch it not, as in many and great affairs. A man may drown in a little brook or pool, as well as in a trreat river, if he lie down and plunge himself into it, and put his head under water. Some care thou must have, that thou mayest not care. Those things that are thorns indeed, thou must make a hedge of them, to keep out those temptations that accompany sloth, and extreme want that waits on it : but let them be the hedge : suffer them not to grow within the garden. þÿ Coleridge.

Drowned but not Dead. þÿ "Captain, þÿ a gentleman of considerable property in the county of Edinburgh, had become insolvent, executed a trust-deed for behoof of his creditors, left Edinburgh, and occasionally resided in France and England. In the month of August 1834, having put up at a hotel at Heme Bay, he went out one morning about seven o'clock to bathe, but never returned ; and his clothes having been found on the beach, it was naturally enough concluded that the Captain had been drowned A proof of the circumstances under which he disappeared seemed no longer doubtful; his son was duly served heir to the entailed estate of þÿ ,and has since exercised the functions of superior in granting new titles, &c. to feuars on the estate. Besides this, various insurances had been effected on the life of Captain þÿ ,both by his creditors, as a body, and by individual creditors for their separate interests ; all of which were premature: Captain þÿ is, it seems, still in the body ; it being ascertained that he was in this city for several weeks in the month of November last, and it is rumoured that he was here much more recently, and sailed in a vessel from Leith to Van Dicmen's Land. This piece of information savours strongly of romance ; but to the creditors and insurance companies it is more than romance. One of the creditors in particular had effected an insurance to the extent of 400/., and had recovered the money ; the creditors, as a body, had effected and recovered ten times that sum, and divided the

each other, were some years ago sent to a public school, when a difficulty arose as to the most familiar way of distinguishing them, A senior boy, having, however, ascertained that the father of one had formerly been a waiter, and the other an auctioneer, suggested that they should be called " Coming Smith" and " Going Smith."

Temperance. þÿ Man was destined to earn his bread by the sweat of his brow, to work for his food. Here there is a provision made for that which is so much neglected by all classes, but those with whom it is part and parcel of their occupation þÿ I mean exercise. Unaided by his fellow-men, destitute as yet of the advantages which a division of labour and commerce supply, his food would of necessity be confined to the few simple herbs which his own toil could extract from the earth, or to the animals which he had earned by his exertions in the chase. Here, then, are two of the first, and the two most important regulations of which modern dietetics in. culcate the observance þÿ namely, exercise and diet. For the best of all reason, a man so situated would not indulge in the use of stimulants: he would not know either that they could be procured or how to procure them ; and, consequently, neither from ale, nor wine, and spirits, would he run any risk. And here we find the third section in nature's scheme of diet þÿ sobriety; and a sobriety, it will be observed, not merely the comparitive degree of drunkenness, but positive temperance, complete abstinence from stimulating liquids. þÿ This, then, may be said, to be the natural state of man þÿ the state in perfect accordance with which his organs were formed, and all the tissues of his body were fashioned and modified." þÿ Robertson on Diet.

GRENADA. From the St. George's Chronicle, Oct. 1.) SLAVE TRADE. Scarcely had the ink ceased to flow from Our pen, when, on Thursday morning, we discried in the distant offing three sail of vessels: the flag at the main-royal mast head of the larger, announced her to be His Majesty's Ship " Vestal," and that her cruise, on which 6he sailed on the 24th, in pursuit of a suspicious vessel, had resulted in the capture, not of one, but two other slavers, and the discharge of eight guns in succession, proclaimed the number on board of both to be 800 or thereabouts. From one of the officers, we learn that the ' Vestal" did not get sight of the vessel of which she went in pursuit, after running 120 miles to the N. W., when returning to the port, at day light on the 28lh, the " Vestal" being about It! miles to the Southward of Point Salines, descried a sail 8 or 10 miles to the S. VV., with which she came up after an interesting chase of four hours ; the " Empresa," with a cargo Spanish chase proved to be the of 434 Africans ; Bntrantine after taking possession, the " Vestal" stood to the Northward At sunset, another suspicious vessel was just in sight from the frigate's deck, running down from the Eastward ; as soon as it became dark, the " Vestal" tacked to intercept her þÿ this was effected at halfpast eight o'clock, and the " Phoenix" Portuguese Brigantine was taken with 486 Africans on board ; the original number was 516, of whom 32 died on the passage. The frigate, and her two prizes came to anchor in the bay on Thursday noon. The " Empresa"

after watering, sailed for the Havanna The " Phoenix" is now in the Carenage, and her cargo w 11 be landed as soon as proper accommodations can be procured. Both of these vessels are of a very superior construction' and appear to possess every requisite to constitute them fast sailers. The "Negrinha" has been refitted, and will proceed next week, in company with the "Phoenix" to Sierra Leone, for adjudication. Here we have an instance, within our personal observation, of no fewer than 1157 of our fellow creatures redeemed from a worse than Egyptian bondage, through the instrumentality of a single vessel, within the limited space of only eurht days 1 We question whether the records of this particular portion of British naval history can furnish a parallel ; certain it is, we know of none. To Captain Jones, his officers, and ship's company, the British public are indebted, the cause of humanity is indebted : but, oh ! how vast the incalculable debt of gratitude due to them by the at once unfortunate and fortunate beings, who reap the fruits of their vigilance þÿ the enjoyment of perfect freedom. Surely the fervent voice of prayer of the sable sons of Africa, and their most remote posterity, will be lifted up to the throne of the Most- High, ingratitude for the benefits which have thus been providentially conferred upon them : that their minds, then hearts, their understandings may be so directed, as to enable them to lift up that voice, is a wish in which we, in common

with every othei member of the human family, should freely indulge. There is much cause to regret that the existing treaty with Spain renders the destination of the "Emprcsa" unavoidable; the impunity with which that nation has heretofore

RAINING FISHES. I acted for some time as chaplain to the 36th Regiment on their return from India, and, chatting one day after dinner at the mess, I asked them did they ever witness that curious phenomenon of ruining fishes, so often but so vagulely mentioned by writers. Several told ine they had frequently found small fishes after heavy rains on the flat roots of the verandahs, but they all concurred in bearing testimony to the following fact : þÿ When they were stationed at Bangalore, and were one day at dinner, the mess-man ran in to tell them the sentry at the mess-room door had reported, that it was raining fishes. They all started up from table, and rushed out to witness the curious phenomenon. A sudden and heavy shower had just passed, but had left behind it several pools in which small fishes were floundering about, and otheis were lying dead where there was no water. One of the officers had taken the precaution to put on his hat before he went out into the rain ; on their return to the mess room a small fish was found in the cock of it. The report of this phenomenon is not confined to India, but similar tilings are recorded to have occurred in our own country. On the Uth of March, 1813, the inhabitants of the island of Uiva, in Argyleshire, were astonisheu to find numbers of small herring-fry strewed over their fields after a shower of rain, so fresh as to be eaten and some of them even in which life was not altogether extinct. A gentleman in the west of Ire-

land, whose veracity 1 have no reason to doubt, assured me he knew such a thing to occur in a farm of his on the sea shore, i ney had drawn up sea-wrack to manure some potatoe-ground, as is usual ; on going out next day to spread it, they found a number of small fishes apparently the fry of sprats or herrings, scattered about on the heaps and on the fielu between them, which afterwards, he supposed, contributed inuch to the feitiiizing property of the sea-.veed. I have never seen these things myself, and the credit of them depends on tiie authority of the narrator. Jides penes auctorem, þÿ are accounted for, They by supposing a waterspout raising them up with the fluid, when a small fry happened to be floating on the surface within the circle of its influence ; and I was w ilness on land to an analogous fact. It was a gusty day, and 1 was watching some columns of dust which the eddies of wind were raising in different parts of the road, and moving troin place to place in miniature representation of those magnificent pillars sand, which travellers describe in of the deserts of Atrica. Suddenly a violent gust came on, and raised it to a considerable height, without breaking the mass. It then dispersed, and was borne along to a great distance, raining hay, straw, and hits of wood heavier than small fishes, lor a mile along the road.
